title: Introduction to interpretation and the legislative process

topics.heading: What the “regulatory state” means
topics.body: Slide 1 defines it, for the course, as governance in which administrative agencies, through rulemaking, monitoring and enforcement, play an expansive role in addressing collective problems and implementing public policy. It quotes Gillian Metzger's fuller account: agencies with broad discretion across rulemaking, adjudication, enforcement and management, the personnel from civil servants to White House overseers, and the institutional arrangements that structure them.

topics.heading: Agenda and course logistics
topics.body: The first class covers the syllabus, the Constitution's allocation of power and the complexity of interpretation, the legislative process, and why that process does not ensure action that follows majority or even super-majority opinion. Slide 3 says the course weighs tools against doctrine and leans to the administrative-law side; three TAs each meet weekly with a third of the class on key slides and ungraded problems with written feedback; students are assigned to six preparation panels; and under NYU rules up to five classes may be missed, with streaming not counting as attendance.

topics.heading: The hierarchy of federal law
topics.body: Agencies may issue regulations if authorized by Congress, which enacts statutes implementing powers granted by the Constitution. Courts may strike down regulations not authorized by statute and statutes not authorized by the Constitution, and interpretation matters at every stage.

topics.heading: Why study legislation and regulation
topics.body: Understanding statutes requires understanding how legislatures work, and understanding regulation requires understanding agencies such as the EPA, SEC, FTC, FCC, SSA and NLRB. Many lawyers appear before agencies and legislatures, and even litigators often argue about statutes and regulations rather than common law. Common law is found in judicial opinions whose force depends on geography and hierarchy; regulatory law starts with statutes, many of which delegate rulemaking to agencies, and more law is now made by legislatures and agencies than by courts.

topics.heading: The puzzles of text
topics.body: Ambiguous statutes require interpretation. Some ambiguity is in the text itself: “intrinsic meaning” has given way to “communities of interpretation”, and ordinary meaning can differ from scientific, legal or dictionary meaning. Other puzzles come from the processes that produce the text.

topics.heading: Introducing Articles I–III
topics.body: Slide 10 asks where Congress gets its power to investigate executive waste, fraud or abuse; whether the President may create a cabinet-level Department of Technological Innovation; whether Congress may maintain a separate Air Force and make the Secretary of Defense its Commander-in-Chief; and whether a President may be impeached and convicted for lesser offences if the punishment is only censure. Slide 11 quotes the Judiciary Act of 1789 on the Attorney General and asks what a “meet person” is and whether Washington could have required a written report on staffing.

topics.heading: Sources of constitutional meaning
topics.body: Theories of government are inferred from the Constitution's structure, the Framers' understanding, the purposes of its provisions and arrangements that have stood the test of time, and from the text. Using the Opinion Clause, the slide asks whether the President may require oral opinions, or the opinion of the head of the FAA inside the Department of Transportation, and raises “the puzzle of the original Attorney General”.

topics.heading: Congress: framework and organization
topics.body: Congress has two Houses, each making its own procedural rules; a statute needs approval of an identical text by both and the President's signature or a veto override. A “Congress” sits for the two years after an election (for example the 119th), usually with one session a year, and each House works through subject-matter committees led by a chairman, with the senior minority member as ranking member. Slides 15 and 16 list the House and Senate committees of the 119th Congress.

topics.heading: The simple model and legislative history
topics.body: In the simple model a legislator proposes a bill, it is referred to committee, which holds hearings, marks it up and reports it, the chamber debates and votes, and a conference committee reconciles different versions. Legislative history comprises drafts, published hearings, committee reports and mark-up, floor debates in the Congressional Record, the conference report and the enrolled bill.

topics.heading: Katzmann: why legislation is often vague or ambiguous
topics.body: Slide 19 lists Katzmann's reasons: problems cannot be foreseen, language is inherently imprecise, Congress decides to delegate broadly and let agencies resolve specific questions later, coalition politics, and congressional organization, including the decentralized committee system.

title: Introduction to regulation and the administrative state

topics.heading: Why the administrative state matters to lawyers
topics.body: After a review of Class 1, Slide 2 gives three reasons: agencies enact more binding rules of conduct than Congress, adjudicate more disputes than all federal courts combined, and impose compliance costs estimated at $1 trillion a year, about a tenth of GDP.

topics.heading: A democratic puzzle: Senate and House procedure
topics.body: Slide 3 asks why Congress does not routinely enact measures backed by overwhelming public majorities. In the Senate, unlimited debate allows filibusters, and cloture takes 60 votes except for reconciliation bills and confirmations. In the House, bills reach the floor under special rules from a Rules Committee dominated by leadership loyalists, and under recent GOP majorities no bill reached the floor without majority-party support (the “Hastert Rule”).

topics.heading: Features of the legislative process
topics.body: Obstacles to legislating are designed to encourage deliberation and input from many constituencies; norms matter; legislators respond to policy preferences, leadership and reelection, party loyalty and available bargains; and collective action problems mean legislation tracks well-organized groups, since small groups with intense interests organize more easily than large diffuse ones (the slide asks how environmental, civil rights and safety laws are then explained). The “vetogates” are committee chairs, floor scheduling, the filibuster, refusal to adopt a conference version, and the veto.

topics.heading: Party discipline and the Senate
topics.body: In the House, leadership controls the agenda through the Rules Committee, and moderates back leadership rules rather than forming cross-party coalitions because of the norm of supporting special rules, the lower cost of going along, and rewards for loyalty. In the Senate, cloture and unanimous consent agreements work around unlimited debate; filibusters can benefit moderates by letting them vote for measures that will not pass or dissent when it does not matter; filibusters were abolished for all presidential nominations.

topics.heading: Budget, reconciliation and the inputs to legislation
topics.body: Spending runs through appropriations and authorizations. A concurrent budget resolution, which cannot be filibustered and is not sent to the President, directs committees to change outlays or revenues by specified amounts over a specified time or to change the debt limit. Slide 13 lists those who shape legislation: voters, executive personnel, committee staff, lobbyists, legislative counsel and the press, who may or may not reflect popular majorities.

topics.heading: Political questions
topics.body: Slide 15 lists the markers of a political question: textual commitment to another branch, lack of manageable standards, a nonjudicial policy determination, lack of respect for other branches, need to adhere to a prior political decision, and potential embarrassment. Slide 16 offers examples to test: a tax bill the Senate voted on first, treaty withdrawal, a retaliatory bombing, receiving an ambassador, and a Senate impeachment trial whose evidence was heard by a committee.

topics.heading: Rucho v. Common Cause
topics.body: In North Carolina the parties split the vote evenly but Republicans won 9 of 12 seats; in Maryland a 65–35 Democratic vote produced 7 of 8 seats, and the motive was openly stated in both. The majority held there is no “limited and precise standard that is judicially discernible and manageable” without a baseline of fairness, since the claims presuppose proportional representation, and pointed to Congress, state courts and initiatives. Kagan's dissent found vote dilution and associational harms, said adjudication of intent, effects and cause would be routine, and called the alternatives illusory. Slide 21 sets out the earlier standards offered by Stevens and by Souter with Ginsburg.

topics.heading: Algal blooms and the limits of private law
topics.body: The case study is algal blooms: causes include agricultural runoff, urban and suburban nutrients, climate change and invasive species; harms include public health, habitats, property values and tourism. The first regime of regulation was the common law, and the slides ask whether contracts with polluters or tort suits would manage the harm. Tort law's limits listed are that it only deters harms that would produce lawsuits, is retrospective and reactive, faces uncertainty, and raises institutional competence, accountability, participation and collective action problems.

topics.heading: Arguments for and against regulation
topics.body: Arguments for include negative externalities, information asymmetries and market concentration, public goods, ending group subordination, intergenerational equity, protecting scarce resources and values for their own sake; the first successful national regulation was of steamboat boilers. Arguments against include costs exceeding benefits, unfairness to regulated parties, unintended effects on innovation and entry, value disputes, and irrational or unfairly adopted choices. Slide 28 separates normative accounts (whether something should happen) from descriptive ones (why it does).

topics.heading: The path to administration
topics.body: Legislatures, given the limits of the common law, often regulate to advance social goals, but “Should there be a regulation?” is a different question from “Should there be a regulatory agency?”. The path runs: is there a problem warranting response, would private law remedies suffice, should the legislature prescribe conduct rules, should an agency be put in charge, and what tools should it have.

topics.heading: Why agencies, and what shapes they take
topics.body: After a recap and the path to administration, the slides list the first departments (Foreign Affairs, War, Treasury, Post Office). Agencies offer focused attention, expertise, early action, efficiency, transparency and accountability, but are less directly accountable, susceptible to capture, prone to self-preserving interests and hard to coordinate. Growth came in spurts: the founding, the maturing national economy, the New Deal, the 1960s–70s social movements, and twenty-first-century crises. Treasury (single head, many sub-agencies) is contrasted with the NLRB (multiple heads, policy mainly by adjudication).

topics.heading: Discretion as the foundational problem
topics.body: Slide 9 names discretion as the foundational problem of administrative law. Slide 10 illustrates levels of discretion with instructions from “Mow my lawn every Saturday to a height of 3/4 inches...” to “Improve my property.” Slide 11 frames it as a principal–agent problem: every statute creates a clear or fuzzy zone of discretion, the agent may not know how the principal wants it used or may act long after enactment, and it is unclear who the principal is: the enacting or sitting Congress, the President, regulated parties or the courts.

topics.heading: Government lawyers and where they look for law
topics.body: The lawyers are in the Justice Department (Attorney General, Solicitor General, Office of Legal Counsel), agency general counsels, and offices and bureaus. They look to the Constitution and cases, organic statutes, authorization and appropriations acts, generic statutes such as the APA, judicial opinions, Attorney General and OLC opinions, executive orders, and agency law in circulars, manuals, precedential orders and rules in the Federal Register and CFR. Slide 14 lists the design challenges: rule of law, process fairness, instrumental rationality, cost-effectiveness, political accountability, interest representation and public values.

topics.heading: Statutory context and the complications of construction
topics.body: Slides 16 and 17 ask whether a command means one must eat any pastry taken with a knife and fork, and whether added text limits a rule or illustrates one application. Interpretation (meaning) differs from construction (application): even if an ambulance is a vehicle, does a ban on vehicles apply to it? Complexity comes from language (ambiguity, vagueness, unforeseen applications, deliberate delegation, coalition fudging) and from institutional roles: Katzmann says judges should be “faithful to the work of the people’s representatives”, which raises whether that means text or purpose, and whether to defer to an agency's prior interpretation.

topics.heading: Structuring the analysis and the three approaches
topics.body: Slide 20 gives the questions for every case: what triggered the suit, what text is disputed, what the contending readings are and why they matter, which the court picks and why. Slide 21 names intentionalism, purposivism and textualism, which use largely the same tools with different emphasis and all start from legislative supremacy.

topics.heading: The hierarchy of federal and New York courts
topics.body: The Supreme Court has nine Justices and discretionary review; 13 courts of appeals hear appeals as of right in three-judge panels, with the D.C. Circuit hearing many agency cases and the Federal Circuit organized by subject; 94 district courts find facts and first review agency action; and specialized tribunals include the Tax Court, Court of International Trade and bankruptcy courts. Many statutes route agency review straight to the courts of appeals, and circuit splits shape agency practice until resolved. Slide 23's New York chart is an image.

topics.heading: Riggs v. Palmer
topics.body: New York's statute made wills final except in the cases it listed (fraud, duress, incapacity), which did not include an heir who murders the testator. The court implied that exception for three reasons: absurdity, the statute's policy, and the common-law rule against profiting from one's own wrong. The dissent invoked legislative supremacy, the testator's intent and the ban on ex post facto penalties. The hypotheticals ask about a grandson who instead kills the grandfather's best friend, or one of the daughters, discovered only after the grandfather's death.

topics.heading: Church of the Holy Trinity v. United States
topics.body: Slide 26 breaks the contract-labor statute into its clauses and tests it with hypotheticals (Chinese lumberjacks bound for Canadian land leased by a Seattle company; English workers reimbursed as far as Nova Scotia). The church hired an English pastor, and the statute's exceptions did not cover clerics. The majority inferred an exception from the title (“labor” as manual labor in ordinary meaning), the aim of protecting American wages, legislative history referring to “cheap, unskilled labor”, and the public-policy passage calling this “a Christian nation”.

topics.heading: Purposivist and textualist premises
topics.body: After a recap of Class 3, Slide 2 contrasts the premises. Purposivists assume Congress acts rationally to achieve its purposes, so laws should be read in light of them because legislatures may act in haste. Textualists treat every statute as a compromise, read misalignments between purpose and detail as bargains, and see fidelity to Congress as fidelity to the bargain, partly because purpose is too slippery when statutes serve many purposes.

topics.heading: Katzmann on legislative history
topics.body: Slide 3 lists Katzmann's points: legislators give legislative history weight, members are more likely to rely on it than to read bill text, committees are representative of the larger body, professional drafters rarely use dictionaries, those who create legislative history value credibility, and drafters pay little attention to canons.

topics.heading: Garland v. Cargill: the question and the statute
topics.body: Slide 4 asks which of two questions you would guess has a “yes” answer: is a bump-stock rifle a “machine gun”, or is a gun kit a “firearm”? In Cargill the question was whether a bump stock converts a semiautomatic rifle into a machinegun, which the Gun Control Act of 1968 bars transferring or possessing. The district court ruled against the owner; the en banc Fifth Circuit reversed, a majority relying on the rule of lenity and a plurality on the definition. Slide 7 quotes 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b).

topics.heading: ATF’s rule and interpretation
topics.body: ATF defined “automatically” as functioning through a self-acting mechanism and “single function of the trigger” as “a single pull of the trigger and analogous motions”, and expressly included bump-stock devices that harness recoil so the trigger resets and keeps firing. On ATF's view, one pull starts a fire–recoil–bump–fire sequence that continues while the shooter keeps a stationary finger and forward pressure on the grip.

topics.heading: Cargill: majority, dissent and the presumption against ineffectiveness
topics.body: The majority held a bump-stock rifle does not fire more than one shot “by a single function of the trigger”, using dictionary definitions; ATF's theory would reach rifles without bump stocks and could not be squared with the Ithaca Model 37 shotgun; and the rifle would not fire “automatically” because it needs precise forward pressure. The dissent said the majority fixates on internal mechanics rather than the human act, relied on contemporaneous usage including the NRA president's testimony, and invoked the presumption against interpretations that facilitate ready evasion. Slide 14 notes there was no deference to ATF, which had concluded the opposite on more than ten occasions before the 2017 Las Vegas shooting.

topics.heading: Bondi v. VanDerStok: statute, issue and rule
topics.body: The question was whether certain weapon parts kits are “firearms”, so that guns built from them need serial numbers; the district court and court of appeals ruled for the manufacturers on a facial challenge. ATF's rule added to the statutory definition “a weapon parts kit that is designed to or may readily be completed, assembled, restored, or otherwise converted to expel a projectile”. ATF's stated reasons were background checks and tracing, given profound recent changes in how guns are made and sold.

topics.heading: VanDerStok: majority, canons and dissent
topics.body: The majority treated “weapon” as an artifact noun defined by intended function, so an ordinary speaker might call a disassembled rifle or a “Buy Build Shoot” kit a weapon, by analogy to starter guns; it cautioned that its Gun Control Act reading says nothing about regulating AR-15 receivers as machineguns under the National Firearms Act. Neither lenity nor constitutional avoidance had a role where “text, context, and structure” decided the case. Justice Thomas's dissent rejected special rules for artifact nouns; the slide lists further dissent arguments omitted from the excerpt.

topics.heading: Letter or spirit: persistent puzzles
topics.body: Slide 24 asks whether judges should follow a statute's letter or spirit, and whether spirit means subjective or imputed intent, objective purpose, or judge-identified public policy. It asks whether any evidence of intent is more compelling than text, how to explain that Congress historically overrides more textualist than purposive decisions, and what fidelity to text means when judges who agree on method disagree on meaning.

topics.heading: The history and hierarchy of legislative history
topics.body: Use grew sporadically from 1860 to 1940, peaked from the 1940s to the mid-1980s (Manning and Stephenson suggest more open-ended statutes and a different view of the judicial role; other explanations are better histories and DOJ's access advantage), and was followed by a textualist resurgence. Sources rank from conference reports, one-house committee reports and sponsor statements, through changes between versions and rejected proposals, floor statements and hearings, to legislative silence and post-enactment activity. The slides ask whether history may be used to show how a word was used, intent on a specific issue, or purpose, and how to weigh sources.

topics.heading: Train v. Colorado PIRG
topics.body: Colorado groups sued EPA under the FWPCA citizen-suit provision for failing to set standards for radioactive effluents from two nuclear plants regulated by the AEC under the Atomic Energy Act, arguing that “pollutant”, which lists “radioactive materials”, covers all of them. Slide 32 contrasts AEC's “as low as is reasonably achievable” standard with FWPCA permits and technology-based limits. The legislative history relied on was a House report's limited reading, the Pastore–Muskie floor colloquy, a defeated House amendment, a conference report that did not challenge the reading and a conferee's echoing statement; the context was the FWPCA's state role and the difference between regulating the nuclear industry and radioactive materials from other activities.

topics.heading: War Powers Resolution problem: the statute
topics.body: The separate War Powers deck quotes the Resolution’s § 1543(a) (without a declaration of war, a written report within 48 hours of introducing forces into hostilities or imminent hostilities, giving circumstances, authority and expected scope and duration); § 1544(b) (forces must be withdrawn within 60 days of a required report unless Congress declares war, specifically authorizes the use, extends the period or cannot meet, with up to 30 more days on certified military necessity); and § 1547(d) (the Resolution neither alters constitutional authority nor grants the President authority he would otherwise lack).

topics.heading: War Powers problem: Libya 2011 and the legislative history
topics.body: The timeline runs from protests in mid-February 2011 and Security Council Resolution 1973, through U.S. strikes two days later, President Obama's March 21 report “consistent with WPR” and an April 1 OLC opinion, to May 20, when 60 days ran without a further report or withdrawal. The administration's position was that its constrained, supporting role in a UN-authorized coalition, without sustained fighting, ground troops, casualties or real risk of escalation, was not “hostilities” under the 60-day provision. Slide 6 quotes H. Rept. 93-287 (1973) on the 1970 Cambodian incursion as the impetus and on the meaning of “war powers”; Slide 7's excerpts are images.

conflicts.heading: The Gun Control Act definition is in Title 18, not Title 28
conflicts.body: Slide 15 heads the VanDerStok definition of “firearm” as “28 U.S.C. § 921(a)”. The assigned VanDerStok reading and the Atlas's entries cite it as 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3).

conflicts.heading: The FWPCA “pollutant” definition is in Title 33
conflicts.body: Slide 31 cites the definition of “pollutant” as “13 U.S.C. § 1362(6)” (and spells the Act “FWCPA”). The Train v. Colorado PIRG opinion in the assigned reading cites it as 33 U.S.C. § 1362(6).

topics.heading: Recap and Katzmann’s tool set
topics.body: For textualists legislative history is controversial: never used to overcome plain meaning, though it may reveal technical meaning or confirm plain meaning; for purposivists it may supply critical context, ranked by reliability. Slide 2 lists Judge Katzmann's tools: text, structure, legislative history, usage in other statutes, common-law usage, agency interpretations, dictionaries, technical and lay usage, common practices, purpose and canons.

topics.heading: United States v. Gayle and Small v. United States
topics.body: Under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1), the dispute was whether “any court” means any U.S. court or any court anywhere, because the predicate conviction was Canadian. Slide 5 sets out the arguments: plain language, dangerousness and the House version against foreign legal differences, the “Federal or State” exceptions, domestic reference of public terms, the Senate report, past practice and lenity. The Second Circuit held only U.S. convictions count; in Small the Supreme Court agreed, assuming domestic concerns absent contrary indication, with Thomas, Scalia and Kennedy dissenting that “any” means “any”.

topics.heading: Murphy and Arlington Central v. Murphy
topics.body: IDEA lets prevailing parents recover “reasonable attorneys’ fees as part of the costs”; the issue was whether that includes expert fees. The Second Circuit (with Katzmann) read Casey, a § 1988 case excluding expert fees, as treating IDEA as a contrast, relied on the conference report, and noted that Congress amended § 1988 to overrule Casey but never amended IDEA's fees provision. The Supreme Court reversed: IDEA is Spending Clause legislation, states need clear notice of obligations, and the text addresses lawyers' fees but not experts'. The dissent relied on the conference report and the direction to GAO to study expert costs.

topics.heading: The legislative history debates
topics.body: Slides 11 and 12 tabulate the arguments to avoid and to use legislative history: only the statute passed through the process, versus history as one more guide; manipulation by inserted fragments, versus delegation to committees; incoherence of “legislative intent”, versus committees' incentives to signal the majority accurately; unrepresentative committees, versus committees more often read than bills; judicial activism, versus language's own elasticity; sloppy drafting, versus legislators' expectation that history will be used; and research costs, versus an untestable claim that ignores benefits.

topics.heading: Canons of construction and semantic canons
topics.body: Canons are principles or presumptions used to derive or create meaning. Semantic canons generalize about language; substantive canons tilt for or against outcomes, either as presumptions of legislative intent or to protect values that transcend it. The semantic canons within a statute are expressio unius, noscitur a sociis, ejusdem generis, consistent meaning of the same phrase, and meaning for every word, with others on punctuation, the last antecedent, “and” versus “or” and “may” versus “shall”. Llewellyn argued that canons cannot justify outcomes because contradictory canons are available; Scalia, Macey and Miller argue that coherent practices can develop.

topics.heading: McBoyle v. United States
topics.body: The question was whether knowingly transporting a stolen airplane violated a ban on interstate transport of a “motor vehicle”, defined to include automobiles, trucks, wagons, motorcycles “or any other self-propelled vehicle not designed for running on rails.” Holmes gave five arguments: ordinary speech, the silence of the legislative history about known airplanes, ejusdem generis from the listed items, older state statutes, and fair warning “in language that the common world will understand”; the slide asks whether the last is semantic or substantive.

topics.heading: Gustafson v. Alloyd Co.
topics.body: The question was whether a stock purchase agreement with misstatements about earnings is a “prospectus” under 15 U.S.C. §§ 77b(10) and 77l. Kennedy's majority reasoned that the contract would otherwise face clearly inapplicable disclosure requirements (consistent meaning) and that “communication” must be read with its companions as a widely disseminated communication (noscitur a sociis; the slide queries “Letter??”). Thomas's dissent said the canon created ambiguity and redundancy and that “prospectus” means different things in different sections; Ginsburg called the consistent-meaning presumption weak. Slide 22 notes the tension between noscitur a sociis and the rule against redundancy.

topics.heading: Noscitur a sociis: illustrations and Jarecki
topics.body: Slide 23 illustrates the canon with a cartoon. Slide 24 gives Jarecki v. G.D. Searle & Co., 367 U.S. 303 (1961): in an excess-profits tax on income from “exploration, discovery, or prospecting”, “discovery” meant income-producing activity in oil, gas and mining, not a pharmaceutical discovery; it asks whether that is a better use of the canon than Gustafson's.

topics.heading: Raila and Dolan: the postal-matter exception
topics.body: The FTCA bars suits for “any claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter”; the question is whether “negligent transmission” covers only damage to mail or also misplaced mail that injures someone. Because loss and miscarriage concern the mail itself, noscitur a sociis suggests the narrower reading, while the Third Circuit construed ambiguity in the waiver of sovereign immunity for the government. In Dolan, Kennedy's majority used the canon and pointed to the FTCA's purpose; Thomas dissented on plain meaning. Other clues are the exception's narrower wording, precedent on postal vehicles, legislative history and absurd results.

topics.heading: Ejusdem generis and People v. Smith
topics.body: Ejusdem generis presumes residual terms are of the same kind as the specific terms before them; it operated in McBoyle, and Sierra Club v. Kenney (Ill. 1981) held that sales of “gravel, sand, earth or other material” from park land do not cover timber. In People v. Smith (Mich. 1975) the question was whether a ban on carrying “a dagger, dirk, stiletto, or other dangerous weapon” covers a military rifle in a vehicle; ejusdem generis requires the same kind as a dagger, and the majority's reading was confirmed by a separate statute on rifles carried with unlawful intent and by an “ordered regulatory regime”. Manning and Stephenson's hypotheticals ask about swords and nunchuks.

conflicts.heading: Raila’s year
conflicts.body: Slide 25 dates Raila v. United States “(2d Cir. 2006)”. The Atlas's Raila entry dates the Second Circuit decision 2004.

topics.heading: Recap: using the interpretive tools
topics.body: Litigated disputes usually present coherent alternative arguments drawn from text and context, so the slides advise identifying the competing readings (or, when planning, the reading that gets the desired outcome and the arguments for and against it), assessing the audience to be persuaded, and relying on more than one tool. Canons are unlikely to dictate outcomes alone: they may point in different directions, are usually rebuttable presumptions, and judges may disagree on whether one applies.

topics.heading: Language within and across statutes
topics.body: In pari materia presumes that statutes on the same subject use words the same way; the slide asks whether that is empirically plausible or justified as a goad to coherence. Within one statute the whole act rule, consistent meaning of identical words (but see General Dynamics Land Systems v. Cline (2004), where “age” in the ADEA means “old age” in one place and chronological age in another) and avoiding surplusage apply, with limited weight for titles and provisos. For disparate acts, Casey (1991) excluded expert fees from “attorney’s fees” in § 1988, as EAJA's “reasonable attorney's fee” excludes them, by looking at unrelated statutes.

topics.heading: Repeal by implication is disfavored
topics.body: A later statute is presumed not to overturn an earlier one unless absolutely necessary to make sense of the later statute. The canon works as a clear statement rule: if Congress wants that result, it must say so clearly.

topics.heading: Constitutional avoidance and Public Citizen
topics.body: Classic avoidance presumes Congress intended the constitutional of two possible readings; Ashwander avoidance avoids a reading that raises a serious constitutional question if another is plausible. Public Citizen v. DOJ avoided a separation-of-powers question by holding that the President did not “use” the ABA committee under the Federal Advisory Committee Act, and In re Cheney, 406 F.3d 723 (D.C. Cir. 2005) (en banc), held that no advisory committee is created when private parties meet officials without a vote or veto. Slide 10 tests three justifications (congressional intent, judicial restraint, constitutional meaning) and the objections to each.

topics.heading: Federalism canons and Gregory v. Ashcroft
topics.body: The background runs from Darby (1941) and Maryland v. Wirtz (1968) through National League of Cities v. Usery (1976) to Garcia (1985), which overruled it 5–4. Gregory asked whether the ADEA bars mandatory retirement of state judges, given its exclusion of elected officials, personal staff and appointees “on the policymaking level”. The majority said judicial retirement age is a decision “of the most fundamental sort” for a sovereign, so the Court must be “absolutely certain” of Congress's intent, and judges are not covered unless the language plainly compels it: Congress must make an intent to upset the federal–state balance “unmistakably clear in the language of the statute.”

topics.heading: Smith v. United States and the rule of lenity
topics.body: Smith offered to trade an automatic weapon for cocaine; the Court held that trading a firearm for drugs “uses” it “during and in relation to” a drug trafficking crime under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1). O'Connor's majority reserved lenity for cases where, after seizing everything from which aid can be derived, the statute remains ambiguous; Scalia's dissent said the issue was at least subject to doubt, which should be resolved for the defendant. The slide asks what justifies the rule.

topics.heading: Other canons rooted in constitutional values
topics.body: Slide 18 lists the presumption against preemption (federalism) and against retroactivity (due process). Slide 19 lists the foreign relations canons: Charming Betsy (acts of Congress should not be read to violate international law if possible) and the presumption against extraterritorial application.

topics.heading: Trump v. Illinois: posture and statute
topics.body: The President called Illinois and Texas National Guard members into federal service in response to sometimes violent protests against immigration enforcement in Chicago. The district court enjoined federalization and deployment, the Seventh Circuit reversed on federalization but upheld the bar on deployment, Justice Barrett referred the stay application to the full Court, and the Court denied the stay 6–3. The statute, 10 U.S.C. § 12406, allows federalizing the Guard on invasion, rebellion, or when “the President is unable with the regular forces to execute the laws of the United States.”

topics.heading: Fact, law and the meaning of “regular forces”
topics.body: When statutory authority depends on facts, someone must find that the triggering facts exist (a question of fact) and assess whether the response fits the statute (a question of law); a hypothetical about choosing a “well-written, well-acted light comedy” asks which the Court said the President got wrong. The majority, persuaded by an amicus brief and the Militia Act's 1902–1908 history, read “regular forces” as the standing professional military. Because the Posse Comitatus Act bars using the military to execute the laws absent express authorization, § 12406(3) likely applies only where the military could legally execute the laws and is unable to.

topics.heading: Protective power and the dissents
topics.body: Federal responses to protests can be seen as executing the laws or as an implicit Article II “protective power”; the executive has long said the Posse Comitatus Act does not limit the latter, and the majority, presuming the same term means the same in related statutes, held that inability to exercise protective power is not inability to “execute the laws” under Title 10. Alito, with Thomas, objected to deciding on an argument not pressed below and said the presumption is not conclusive; Kavanaugh warned that the majority would force the President to use the military to protect federal functions however impracticable. Slides 31 to 33 quote the Insurrection Act, 10 U.S.C. §§ 251–253.

conflicts.heading: “Trump v. U.S.” on slides 20 and 21
conflicts.body: Slides 20 and 21 head the National Guard case “Trump v. U.S.”. Slide 24 and the Atlas name it Trump v. Illinois (2025).

topics.heading: Recap of Class 6
topics.body: Canons evolve from judicial decisions and may embody substantive values; constitutional avoidance relieves the Court of resolving a constitutional issue. Canons may conflict, Justices may differ on when they are triggered, and it is hard to ignore the possibility that unstated context shapes the choice and application of method.

topics.heading: Epic Systems v. Lewis: facts and posture
topics.body: Workers claimed they were misclassified as professional employees to deny them overtime under the FLSA, but had signed, apparently as a condition of employment, agreements requiring individualized arbitration before an arbitrator who could grant any relief a court could. The district court compelled arbitration, the Ninth Circuit reversed, and certiorari was granted. The collective options given up were class arbitration, Rule 23 class actions and FLSA collective actions under 29 U.S.C. § 216, which lets employees sue for themselves and others similarly situated.

topics.heading: Gorsuch’s majority: the Arbitration Act
topics.body: The slide describes the majority as textualism, perhaps in service of a perceived purpose. FAA § 2 makes written arbitration provisions valid and enforceable save on grounds for revoking any contract. The § 1 exclusion for seamen, railroad employees and “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce” has been limited by ejusdem generis to transport workers. On the saving clause, Gorsuch held that illegality must be a ground applying to any contract, not one aimed at arbitration; Thomas's concurrence said revocation grounds concern the making of the contract.

topics.heading: Canons for multi-statute problems
topics.body: Slide 9 lists the harmony canon (courts must strive “to give effect to both” Acts), the presumption against implied repeal, the rule that a later irreconcilable statute prevails, and the rule that a specific statute is not controlled by a general one.

topics.heading: Harmonizing the FAA and the NLRA
topics.body: The majority held that NLRA § 7 (29 U.S.C. § 157), protecting “concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection”, does not create a right to class-wide litigation or arbitration; by ejusdem generis and the Act's structure it covers how employees associate in the workplace. Its other tools were comparison with statutes that expressly bar mandatory arbitration, the principle that Congress does not “hide elephants in mouseholes”, and stare decisis, which the slide notes is stronger in statutory cases.

topics.heading: Ginsburg’s dissent and the retorts
topics.body: Ginsburg would harmonize the statutes by reading the FAA as aimed at business-to-business contracts between parties of comparable bargaining power and the NLRA as redressing workers' imbalance. She argued that NLRA illegality targets individualized arbitration, not arbitration; that the canon should not defeat Congress's intended breadth (the majority answered that legislative history is not law); that later specific procedures do not limit § 7; that § 7 allows group complaints to agencies that did not exist in 1935; and that the NLRA is the more specific statute on group action. The majority said the dissent resorts to policy; the dissent warned of billions in wage theft.

topics.heading: The nondelegation problem
topics.body: The agenda for Classes 7 and 8 is what the nondelegation doctrine is, why Congress delegates broadly and courts do not enforce the doctrine more stringently, why Justice Scalia's majority rejected the D.C. Circuit's approach, and how an administrative lawyer can still use it. The premises are that no branch may usurp another's powers or abdicate its own, and that a principal must accept some discretion in its agent; the problem is distinguishing inevitable discretion from abdication. Slides 20 and 21 show the zone of discretion between ultra vires acts and the lawn-mowing levels of discretion.

topics.heading: The Brig Aurora and Marshall Field v. Clark
topics.body: In the Brig Aurora (1813) the President could revive a ban on British or French imports on finding that either had not changed its edicts; it was approved because the President proclaims a fact that triggers the law. In Field (1892) the President could suspend free trade in sugar, molasses, coffee, tea and hides when a nation treated U.S. goods in a manner “reciprocally unequal and unreasonable”, for such time “as he shall deem just”; it was approved on precedent, as fact-finding that triggers a duty, with the President “the mere agent of the law-making department”, and because discretion as to execution is not lawmaking.

topics.heading: United States v. Grimaud and Wayman v. Southard
topics.body: Grimaud (1911) upheld rules for forest reservations, enforced against defendants grazing sheep without a licence: once Congress had indicated its will, it could give those acting under it “power to fill up the details”, though the Secretary “could not make rules and regulations for any and every purpose.” The Court quoted Wayman v. Southard (1825) that Congress cannot delegate powers “strictly and exclusively legislative” but may delegate powers it could exercise itself; the slide asks whether the category depends on what is done or who does it.

topics.heading: J. W. Hampton v. United States and the intelligible principle
topics.body: Hampton (1928) upheld presidential adjustment of tariffs to equalize foreign and domestic costs of production after investigation. The scope of delegation follows “common sense and the inherent necessities of government coordination”, and if Congress lays down “an intelligible principle” to which the delegate must conform, there is no forbidden delegation. Like Field, nothing about the legislation's expediency or just operation was left to the President, who acted with a Tariff Commission's advice.

topics.heading: Schechter Poultry v. United States
topics.body: The NIRA let the President approve or prescribe codes of fair competition, here covering hours, wages, labour conditions, trade practices and reporting in the live poultry industry, subject only to not creating barriers to entry or monopoly and such conditions as he deemed necessary. The Court found no adequate definition of the subject, no standards for any industry, virtually unfettered discretion, and a “finding” that was really an opinion about the general effect of a scheme of laws. Slide 34 quotes the NIRA's long policy section.

topics.heading: Yakus v. United States
topics.body: Yakus (1944) upheld wartime price controls letting the Price Administrator fix prices that “in his judgment will be generally fair and equitable and will effectuate the purposes of this Act” when prices had risen or threatened to rise inconsistently with those purposes, which Slide 36 lists. The Court would override Congress only if standards were so absent that it would be impossible to ascertain whether Congress's will had been obeyed.

conflicts.heading: Hampton’s initials
conflicts.body: Slides 28 to 30 name the case “J.R. Hampton, Jr. & Co. v. U.S.” The Atlas names it J. W. Hampton, Jr., & Co. v. United States (1928).

topics.heading: Recap: discretion and the Court’s tests
topics.body: Textualists and purposivists both claim to be Congress's faithful servants; the supposed difference is the range of tools judges may use. The central rule-of-law problem of administrative law is discretion, and the Court has struggled to say how much Congress may convey without abdicating, using fact-finding versus lawmaking, primary policymaking versus filling up details, and discretion bound by an “intelligible principle”. Slides 4 to 6 repeat Yakus from Class 7.

topics.heading: Mistretta v. United States and Scalia’s dissent
topics.body: The Sentencing Commission was to avoid unjustified disparities and address four needs: just punishment and respect for law, deterrence, protecting the public, and providing training, care or treatment. The delegation was approved because Congress set the policies, the tool (a guideline system), its general shape, starting points and factors, leaving detailed expert work suited to an administrative body. Scalia's dissent said the Commission makes law, not policy within an administrative scheme, so the issue is not the specificity of standards but naked lawmaking. Slide 10 asks whether a hypothetical delegation to the President to define crimes and penalties differs from Mistretta.

topics.heading: Amalgamated Meat Cutters v. Connally
topics.body: The statute let the President issue orders stabilizing prices, rents, wages and salaries at no less than May 25, 1970 levels, with adjustments to prevent gross inequities. Judge Leventhal upheld it on a menu of factors, and the slide asks whether they measure the same thing: narrowing terms and past price administrations show it is not a blank check; and it need not cause alarm given reasoned analysis, the link to trade posture, short duration, exigent circumstances, implicit requirements of fairness and intelligible policy, and pre-enforcement judicial review.

topics.heading: The border fence waiver and policy as tradeoffs
topics.body: Section 102(c) of IIRIRA, as amended in 2005, lets the Secretary of Homeland Security waive “all legal requirements” the Secretary, in sole discretion, finds necessary for expeditious construction of border barriers. Government standards embody tradeoffs between competing values, and the more discretion the executive gets, the more of those tradeoffs it makes. Reasons to want Congress to make them include the separation of powers, forced consensus, electoral accountability, clearer direction to agencies, less regulatory law and perhaps transparency.

topics.heading: How to set limits, and why Congress delegates
topics.body: A formalist approach draws a bright-line distinction between legislation and execution; a pragmatic one asks about control and accountability: the scope and duration of the action, the breadth of the delegation and whether a narrower one is practicable, and procedural guarantees. Congress delegates for speed in crises, executive expertise and resources, national coherence, early action, flexibility (a statute can be changed only by statute), credit-taking and buck-passing, and members' hope of influencing an agency. Courts hold back because vague laws empower interpretation, judges are unelected, courts can only tear down, other doctrines exist, Congress is not usurping power, and no specificity standard is objective.

topics.heading: Whitman v. American Trucking: EPA’s approach
topics.body: The Clean Air Act requires air standards “requisite to protect the public health … with an adequate margin of safety”; ozone and probably particulate matter are nonthreshold pollutants, and zero exposure is not feasible. EPA's approach set the level by the severity and likelihood of effects and population affected: at or below the lowest concentrations associated with significant effects, above natural background, where effects are likely transient, reversible and endured by very few, using the latest science and deferring to scientific consensus on seriousness. The Court held economic factors may not be considered: the text is directive and silent on costs, no provision clearly authorizes them, Congress hides no elephants in mouseholes, and avoidance has no role absent ambiguity.

topics.heading: The D.C. Circuit’s theory and the Supreme Court’s answer
topics.body: The D.C. Circuit held EPA's rule failed nondelegation because it set no actual limits on EPA's choice, but that EPA could save the statute by adopting limits. Slide 25 scores that idea against the doctrine's purposes: an agency's own limiting principle prevents arbitrary action and enables review (yes) but does not leave fundamental policy choices to Congress (no). The Supreme Court held unconstitutional statutes cannot be saved by agency self-restriction, and that this statute was sufficiently determinate compared with precedent.

topics.heading: Gundy v. United States
topics.body: The Court had already read SORNA to apply to pre-enactment offenders; since Congress may have thought immediate registration impossible, the implicit requirement was for the Attorney General to apply it to them as soon as feasible, read from purpose, history and text, with feasibility meaning administrative and temporary authority. The plurality found an intelligible principle; Alito concurred as no worse than earlier cases but willing to reconsider. Gorsuch's dissent found no textual limit and, on the Framers' categorical understanding, would allow only filling up details, finding contingent facts, and adding to existing Article II discretion.

topics.heading: History and defences of broad delegation
topics.body: Parrillo's history shows early Congresses repeatedly gave significant rulemaking discretion; the riposte is that early examples were non-coercive, foreign-affairs related or fact-finding, and the surrebuttal that no one argued for such exceptions at the founding. Mashaw argues broad discretion lets presidential elections carry voter preferences; Spence and Cross argue Congress cannot legislate specifically, especially for updates, and that agencies are more democratic, expert and harder to manipulate than courts. Slide 32 sets out the tradeoffs: relaxing the doctrine gains expertise and speed but weakens electoral accountability and invites symbolic legislation, while a robust doctrine may tempt judicial activism.

title: Executive branch organization and presidential appointment powers

topics.heading: Recap: the intelligible principle and Congress’s control
topics.body: Despite the discomfort of what may be a majority of the current Justices, the intelligible-principle requirement remains the only judicially enforced limit on delegation, and the Supreme Court rejected the lower court's “non-arbitrariness” version. Congress keeps struggling for control after enactment through oversight, appropriations and confirmation hearings; the legislative veto, designed to bolster its influence, was struck down in Chadha, and other statutes (the CRA, the Impoundment Control Act, the Antideficiency Act) try to sustain its role with debated effect.

topics.heading: Residual effects of nondelegation and over-specific statutes
topics.body: The doctrine survives as a backup in statutory construction: prefer a reading that does not make a statute constitutionally suspect; and some functions, such as a “U.S. Impeachment Agency”, are surely nondelegable. Over-specific statutes are inflexible: a rule may capture cases outside Congress's purposes and become hard to revise as thinking changes, and courts have few tools to police either breadth or narrowness.

topics.heading: The Murry conundrum and irrebuttable presumptions
topics.body: Congress disqualified from food stamps any household containing a member 18 or older claimed as a tax dependent in another household, aiming at middle- and upper-class college students; the slide drafts an alternative delegating the judgment to the Secretary of Agriculture. The Court held the statute an irrational irrebuttable presumption because those disqualified could not show it was inaccurate in their case. The doctrine threatened every statutory category, such as driving ages and progressive tax rates, and would have required adjudication of individual exceptions. Slide 10 concludes that nondelegation has not been used to strike a statute since 1935 and the irrebuttable presumption doctrine is dead.

topics.heading: FCC v. Consumers’ Research (2025)
topics.body: Section 254(d) of the 1996 Telecommunications Act requires carriers to contribute on an equitable and nondiscriminatory basis to the FCC's universal-service mechanisms. Consumers' Research argued the contributions were taxes requiring a definite or objective limit such as a numeric cap; the Court reversed 6–3, holding there is no such special rule and § 254 meets the intelligible-principle test, and upheld subdelegation of the fund's management to the Universal Service Administrative Company because the FCC keeps all decision-making authority. Slide 12 lists recommended public-affairs blogs on separation of powers and administrative law.

topics.heading: Designing the executive branch and reorganization
topics.body: Quoting Mashaw, the 1787 Constitution “left a hole where administration might have been”: it provides a President, executive departments with heads, principal and inferior officers and modes of appointment, and the Necessary and Proper Clause implies Congress's primary role in structuring administration. From 1939 Reorganization Acts gave presidents time-limited power to restructure agencies, subject to a legislative veto, by concurrent resolution and, under the 1977 Act, by one House; after the 1983 ruling against legislative vetoes, presidents since 1984 may only propose reorganizations for ordinary enactment. Agency location shapes culture, as with public lands split between Interior and Agriculture and the 2002 creation of DHS.

topics.heading: The unitary executive debate
topics.body: Presidents have direct constitutional powers (pardons, treaties) and statutory ones (tariffs, with subdelegation under 3 U.S.C. § 301), but many statutes vest discretion in other officials, raising whether the President may direct how they exercise it, on authority from Congress, the Vesting Clause or the Take Care Clause. Unitary executive theory holds that Article II guarantees control of discretionary functions, in flavours from removal of principal officers to personal execution of the laws. Slide 20 sets out the Roberts Court's narrative (the one-person branch, the unbroken chain of command, conclusive and preclusive power in Trump v. United States (2024)); Slides 21 and 22 give Shane's contrary reading and a checks-and-balances model in which the designated officer exercises statutory discretion and the President persuades, firing only if Congress permits.

topics.heading: The Appointments Clause
topics.body: Whether removal and appointment powers are analytically linked to directive control has never been directly tested. The Appointments Clause expresses four modes: the President with advice and consent for all principal and some inferior officers, and, for inferior officers as Congress determines, the President alone, heads of departments or courts of law.

topics.heading: Buckley v. Valeo and who is an officer
topics.body: The FEC had two members appointed by the Senate President pro tem, two by the Speaker and two by the President, with the Senate Secretary and House Clerk ex officio, and exercised enforcement, rulemaking, adjudication, eligibility and advisory powers. Buckley argued that anyone doing that work is an officer who must be appointed under Article II. Officer status turns on function: rules, advisory opinions, prosecution, grants and going to court differ from investigation and clearinghouse work; an officer performs pursuant to law a significant function that could not be delegated to a congressional committee. Slide 28 contrasts Buckley's exclusive reading of the Clause with Congress's argument that its modes are illustrative absent the word “only”.

title: Appointments and presidential removal power before the Roberts Court

topics.heading: Puzzles of Buckley
topics.body: Officers exercise “significant functions pursuant to public law” (Buckley); there is one method for principal officers and four for inferior officers. Would an agency limited to rulemaking and quasi-adjudication have come out differently? No: the test is not the abstract nature of the power but whether Congress could have delegated it to one of its own committees. The Court treats the Appointments Clause as exclusive, though it does not say so, because the Constitution separates legislation from administration, pointing also to the Incompatibility Clause. Slide 3 lists the Civil Rights Commission's functions (investigation, study, clearinghouse, advisory committees, hearings, subpoenas enforced through the Attorney General) as a test case.

topics.heading: Officers or employees: Freytag and Lucia
topics.body: In Freytag (1991) the Tax Court's special trial judges held statutory positions with more than ministerial tasks and significant discretion; in Lucia (2018) the SEC's administrative law judges were held to be officers.

topics.heading: Principal or inferior: Morrison and Edmond
topics.body: Morrison v. Olson, 487 U.S. 654, 671–72 (1988), declined to draw the exact line but found the independent counsel inferior because she was removable by a higher executive official, had limited duties without authority to formulate policy, and had limited jurisdiction. Edmond (1997), unanimously through Justice Scalia, upheld the Secretary of Transportation's appointment of civilian judges of the Coast Guard Court of Criminal Appeals on a formal test that a balancing test would also pass, and the PCAOB case (2010) followed Edmond.

topics.heading: United States v. Arthrex
topics.body: The Secretary of Commerce appointed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's judges, who conducted inter partes review of patents (triggered by anyone, with the presidentially appointed Director designating three judges), with appeal to the Federal Circuit. The Court held that the Director “is the boss, except when it comes to the one thing that makes the APJs officers”, that Federal Circuit review outside Article II cannot supply supervision, and that review by the Director best fits the PTO's structure. Gorsuch would simply have thrown out the decision; Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan found adequate functional justification; Thomas, with them, said APJs are supervised and do not become principal officers because of their decisions.

topics.heading: The chain-of-command theory and legitimacy
topics.body: The Court's normative theory, quoting Free Enterprise Fund, is that executive power acquires legitimacy and accountability through “a clear and effective chain of command” down from the President. Slide 11 separates popular from moral legitimacy and lists other possible sources: the electoral connection, fidelity to statute, procedural fairness, sound decision-making, and responsiveness to circumstances and public input on the ground.

topics.heading: Where the Court leaves appointments
topics.body: Inferior officers are supervised and directed by principal officers, so an officer whose decision binds the executive branch as its final position is not inferior; non-officers are employees whose hiring Congress may provide for by any necessary and proper process. On interbranch appointments, Morrison found nothing suggesting the Framers barred them, but held a court appointment improper if “incongruous” with judicial functions. Slide 16 contrasts Shane (no textual bar, and an uncertain executive–judicial boundary in 1787) with McGinnis (either the judiciary appoints all inferior officers or decides its own limits, transferring control to an unaccountable body).

topics.heading: What makes an agency “independent”
topics.body: Traditionally an agency was independent because its heads were protected by statute from removal at will, removable only for good cause (inefficiency, neglect, malfeasance), usually read to exclude mere policy disagreement with the President. Independent and executive agencies differ in organization, but removal provisions are not uniform, functions are not distinguishable in principle, and politics can surprise.

topics.heading: Myers v. United States and the Decision of 1789
topics.body: Myers invalidated a law requiring Senate advice and consent to fire postmasters, comparable to the Tenure of Office Act behind Johnson's impeachment. The historical argument is the Decision of 1789: the Foreign Affairs bill dropped “to be removable by the President” for language assuming presidential removal. The House held four positions (impeachment only; removal follows appointment; removal by statute; plenary Article II power); Madison probably chose the weaker clause to avoid denying the Senate a role explicitly, and the Senate split 10–10 on it, as Shugerman's work on Maclay's diaries explores.

topics.heading: Myers’s vesting and functional arguments
topics.body: Taft reasoned that statutory duties come under the President's general administrative control through the vesting of executive power, for the “unitary and uniform execution of the laws”, and that the President needs “a reserve power of removal” to enforce the law. He allowed that some duties may be so specifically committed to an officer, or so quasi-judicial, that the President cannot control a particular decision, yet may remove the officer afterwards for unwise exercise of discretion. In dicta, removal of inferior officers is incident to appointment, so Congress may give department heads removal power.

conflicts.heading: “Fair Enterprise Fund” on slide 6
conflicts.body: Slide 6 calls the PCAOB case “Fair Enterprise Fund v. Public Company Accounting Oversight Board”. Slide 10 quotes the same decision as Free Enterprise Fund, 561 U.S. 477 at 498.

title: The Roberts Court and presidential removal power

topics.heading: Myers’s holding and dicta
topics.body: After a recap of Class 10, Slide 2 tabulates Taft's views: Congress may not require a Senate role in removing officers appointed with advice and consent; principal officers and inferior officers appointed with advice and consent must be removable at will; for inferior officers the President appoints alone he leans to at-will removal but leaves it open; and for inferior officers appointed by department heads or courts, removal goes with the appointing official and may be limited by statute.

topics.heading: Humphrey’s Executor
topics.body: A unanimous, ideologically diverse Court held that Congress may limit removal of FTC commissioners to good cause. Its framework treats a postmaster as purely executive and the FTC as exercising quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial powers, confining Myers to purely executive officers. Slide 4 quotes the passage calling the FTC not “an arm or an eye of the executive”, exercising any executive function only in carrying out its quasi-legislative or quasi-judicial powers.

topics.heading: Bowsher v. Synar
topics.body: The Comptroller General could be removed by impeachment or by joint resolution. The President's legal obligations can be created only by Congress through legislation, by courts, or by officers of the United States. Congress argued that impeachment need not be the exclusive means of removal, citing the Necessary and Proper Clause and the lack of real aggrandizement; the Court rejected this, holding that Congress cannot make binding policy by controlling executive functions through removal leverage.

topics.heading: Morrison v. Olson: the independent counsel
topics.body: The Ethics in Government Act required the Attorney General, on specific information of a felony by a covered high official, to investigate for 90 days and, unless he found no need for more, to apply to a special D.C. Circuit panel to appoint an independent counsel, removable only by the Attorney General personally and only for good cause or incapacity. The Court rejected Olson's claim that prosecutors must be under plenary presidential control: the test is whether the restriction impedes the President's ability to perform his constitutional function, good-cause removal lets the President ensure faithful execution, and controlling the counsel's discretion is not central to the executive's functioning.

topics.heading: Opinions not written, and what Morrison implies
topics.body: Slide 11 sketches two unwritten opinions: a balancing approach upholding the Act as narrowly tailored to conflicts of interest within the executive (Watergate), and a historical argument that the founders did not see prosecution as unambiguously executive. Slide 12 reads Morrison as splitting a prosecutor's job into following the law, which removal for cause secures, and exercising discretion that Congress, not the Constitution, vests in the officer. Slide 13 notes Morrison concerned an inferior officer and asks whether removal limits on principal officers categorically impede the President, answering not if Humphrey's is still good law, and quoting the PCAOB decision that a multimember body may head a department.

topics.heading: Scalia’s one-person branch and the text it ignores
topics.body: Scalia's Morrison dissent read the Vesting Clause to give the President “all of the executive power”. Slide 15 answers with other text: the legislative vesting clause says “herein granted”, the Opinions Clause, and the Necessary and Proper Clause's reach to powers vested in any department or officer. Slide 16 lists good-cause provisions for the MSPB, CPSC, Competitiveness Policy Council and Sentencing Commission, and notes that the SEC statute has none.

topics.heading: Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB
topics.body: The PCAOB registers, regulates in detail, inspects, investigates and disciplines accounting firms; willful violation of its rules is a federal crime, and it can revoke registration and impose penalties up to $15 million. The SEC approves its rules and sanctions but can remove members only for good cause, and SEC commissioners are themselves assumed removable only for cause. The Court held that two layers of for-cause protection violate Article II and severed the Board members' protection, leaving them removable at will by the SEC. Slides 21 and 22 chart what the President could do before and after, and Slide 23 explains severability.

topics.heading: Seila Law v. CFPB: the majority
topics.body: The CFPB had FTC-like powers but a single director removable only for “inefficiency, malfeasance, or neglect of office”, with a long term and Federal Reserve funding. The majority rooted removal power in the vesting of “all” executive power and the Take Care Clause, the Decision of 1789, Myers and the novelty of the structure, treating Humphrey's (multimember expert bodies balanced by party) and Morrison (inferior officers with limited duties) as the only exceptions, and calling Humphrey's categorization no longer tenable. It quoted the Framers on an energetic, single, nationally elected executive and severed the removal limit, noting Congress could make the CFPB multimember.

topics.heading: Kagan’s dissent in Seila Law
topics.body: Kagan said Taft's history was almost entirely dicta, Myers was later followed only on Senate consent, and Humphrey's was unanimous with Hughes, Brandeis, Cardozo and Stone. Morrison itself compared the counsel to for-cause agencies with civil enforcement powers. She denied a fixed view in 1789, said novelty is no test (the Necessary and Proper Clause is not “a Rinse and Repeat Clause”), and relied on text (no removal power, the Opinions Clause, faithful execution as a duty), Blackstone, Madison and Story, parliamentary practice, state constitutions, the Sinking Fund Commission, whose members included the Vice President and Chief Justice, and Manning's scholarship. Slide 39 asks whether a multimember CFPB would leave the President better off.

topics.heading: Collins v. Yellen
topics.body: Collins (2021) applied Seila Law to the head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency: “the nature and breadth of an agency’s authority is not dispositive.” Sotomayor, with Breyer, objected that the Court had never forbidden for-cause tenure for an officer who neither exercises significant executive power nor regulates private parties; Kagan also dissented from the extension. Slide 42, on the aftermath in the Biden administration, is an image.

conflicts.heading: “Fair Enterprise Fund” on slide 13
conflicts.body: Slide 13 again attributes the multimember-head quotation to “Fair Enterprise Fund v. Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (2010)”. Slide 17 of the same deck names the case Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB.
