title: Other aspects of presidential control of the bureaucracy

topics.heading: Recap and Trump v. Wilcox
topics.body: Morrison reaffirmed Humphrey's Executor in a somewhat opaque opinion with a broad view of interbranch appointments; the Roberts Court then cut back both, barring double for-cause protection (Free Enterprise Fund) and giving the President plenary removal of single agency heads (Seila Law, Collins). In Trump v. Wilcox (2025) the President fired MSPB chair Cathy Harris and NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox; the district court restored them, the D.C. Circuit declined a stay, and the Supreme Court granted one while describing the Federal Reserve as “a uniquely structured, quasi-private entity” in the tradition of the First and Second Banks.

topics.heading: Trump v. Slaughter: the Roberts opinion
topics.body: At the start of the second Trump administration the FTC had three Democratic members, including the chair, who resigned; the President named a Republican chair and fired the other two Democrats, and the lower courts followed Humphrey's. Resting again on Myers, Chief Justice Roberts reasoned that the Framers chose a unitary presidency, inferior officers were meant to be subordinate, the Decision of 1789 and later presidents confirmed it, Humphrey's rested on a “fictional” view of the FTC, and the main reliance interest is the people's liberty. The opinion does not decide the status of Article I courts and rejects the dissent's history and stare decisis.

topics.heading: Gorsuch’s concurrence and Sotomayor’s dissent
topics.body: Gorsuch said independent agencies exercise all three kinds of power with hardly any statutory guidance, that Slaughter lets the President control all of it, and that presidential power may become more than the sum of its parts, threatening civil-service independence; “electoral accountability is a good thing, it cannot be the only thing”, so the Court must enforce the separation of powers more firmly. Sotomayor traced congressional insistence on independence from the Revolutionary War debt commission and the Banks through the Comptroller of the Currency, ICC, FTC and Federal Reserve; called Humphrey's a 90-year precedent reaffirmed in Wiener and Morrison; noted removal is not in the text or convention debates; and said independent agencies already face presidential influence and were built in reliance on Humphrey's.

topics.heading: Anti-removability originalists and the use of history
topics.body: Slides 11 to 13 list scholars: Mortenson (Article II executive power did not include removal or royal prerogatives), Steilen and Chabot (the Crown was not the model), Shugerman (the Decision of 1789 was inconclusive, the Take Care Clause grants no power, vesting does not imply indefeasibility), Donahue and Rosenblum (the quasi categories were long recognized), and Caleb Nelson (the commission requirement, and a 1789 warning against readings that legalize “a tyrannical disposition”). Slide 14 asks whether the Court was overconfident in its history and when executive-power contests should be political questions.

topics.heading: The Federal Reserve: Trump v. Cook
topics.body: Wilcox hinted the Court would not allow at-will removal of Federal Reserve governors. The President purported to fire Dr. Cook “for cause”; the only question was whether to stay the order below in her favour, and the slide reports holdings that the removal is judicially reviewable and that she was entitled to at least a rudimentary hearing. Slide 16 quotes the Court that the Fed keeps the principles of the First and Second Banks, that monetary policy should not be subject to political interference. Slide 17 asks whether independence can be justified where the Founders could not have foreseen the field, such as digital communications, atomic energy, carcinogens or vaccines.

topics.heading: Multimember agencies, adjudicators, civil servants and quorum
topics.body: Slide 18 gives then-Judge Kavanaugh's reasons multimember structures guard against arbitrariness: no single member can do much, members need a majority, deliberation is fuller, extremes are resisted, dissents monitor both sides, and capture is harder. The Slaughter majority says it does not decide the fate of Tax Court and Court of Federal Claims judges, yet says enforcing a mandate against private parties is executive power “no ifs, ands, or quasis”. The Court treats Perkins (a naval cadet engineer) as protecting only inferior officers with limited duties, raising whether it protects agency professionals whose advice shapes policy. Slide 21 asks what remedies could stop removals used to end bipartisanship or leave agencies without a quorum.

topics.heading: NLRB v. Noel Canning and recess appointments
topics.body: The Recess Appointments Clause lets the President fill “vacancies that may happen during the recess of the Senate” with commissions expiring at the end of the next session; Slides 24 and 25 compare intrasession and intersession recesses to an MBA calendar. On January 4, 2012 the President recess-appointed Richard Cordray to the CFPB and three NLRB members while the Senate, with the House refusing adjournment, held pro forma sessions every few days. The Court answered three questions yes: intrasession recesses count, vacancies need not first arise during the recess, and pro forma sessions broke the period into adjournments too short to be recesses. Practice supported it: use regardless of when vacancies arose since Madison, intrasession appointments since the 1920s, the Pay Act, a ten-day convention, and pro forma sessions since 2005.

topics.heading: The Federal Vacancies Reform Act and acting officials
topics.body: Under 5 U.S.C. § 3345, when a Senate-confirmed executive officer dies, resigns or cannot serve, the first assistant acts, unless the President directs another Senate-confirmed official, or a senior agency employee who served at least 90 days in the prior year at GS-15 pay or above, to act, within § 3346's time limits. Section 3349c excludes members of multimember boards governing independent establishments, FERC and Surface Transportation Board members, and Article I judges. Slide 33 lists unconventional uses: an outside acting CFPB head and a non-confirmed acting Attorney General (Trump I), a Labor Department statute keeping a deputy as acting secretary (Biden), and multi-hat acting appointments (Trump II).

topics.heading: The civil service and Schedule F
topics.body: Slide 34 compares the competitive service (examination, robust notice and hearing), the excepted service (about a third, with protections for preference-eligible or post-probationary employees) and the Senior Executive Service. The Schedule F order would have moved career employees in confidential or policy positions out of removal protections; Biden revoked it on 1/22/2021, and it returned by order on 1/20/25 as Schedule P/C (“Schedule Professional/Career”, Executive Order 14171), with implementing rules not yet final, while Executive Order 14317 created Schedule G for noncareer policy positions. The contested text is 5 U.S.C. § 7511(b)(2), excluding positions determined to be of a confidential, policy-determining, policy-making or policy-advocating character.

file: Class 13 - More on POTUS - Introducing Procedural Modes Under the Constitution and the APA - 10-14-26.pptx
title: Presidential direction and procedural modes under the Constitution and the APA

topics.heading: Presidential authority and directive power
topics.body: Identify whether the proposed direction rests on Article II, express authorization to supervise, or a statute that places discretion in another officer. The EPA trading system, bilingual education and CDC pamphlet hypotheticals test the unsettled third branch. Presidential involvement leaves the agency subject to its statutory limits.

topics.heading: Executive orders and centralized review
topics.body: The lecture traces a typical order from a lead agency draft through OMB circulation and Justice Department legal review. Executive Order 12866 illustrates a distinct review system for agency rules, including regulatory planning, centralized review and dispute resolution.

topics.heading: Youngstown’s competing readings
topics.body: Jackson’s three positions turn on congressional authorization, silence or opposition. The Venn diagram places Article I alongside Article II to visualize possible overlap. Compare Black’s need for legal authority, Frankfurter’s historical gloss, Clark and Burton’s attention to the tools Congress enacted and declined, and the dissent’s appeal to statutory purposes in an emergency.

topics.heading: Layers of procedural protection
topics.body: Work down from constitutional minima through generally applicable statutes, the organic act and agency regulations. The Fifth Amendment governs federal agencies and the Fourteenth Amendment governs state action. Identifying a protected deprivation and determining the procedure it requires are separate steps.

topics.heading: Individual assessments and general policies
topics.body: Londoner required a meaningful chance to support objections before separately determined paving assessments became final. Bi-Metallic rejected an individual constitutional hearing for a citywide revaluation. Ask whether the decision turned on facts about particular parties or on general premises used to set policy.

topics.heading: Hearing format and APA pathways
topics.body: A hearing can take several forms, including written submissions. The deck maps § 551 definitions to rulemaking under § 553 and formal adjudication under § 554. A statutory on-the-record hearing trigger leads to §§ 556–557. Identify the trigger and any independent sources of procedure for the particular agency action.

conflicts.heading: Noel Canning’s short-recess presumption
conflicts.body: The recap uses a categorical ten-day shorthand. Noel Canning held that a recess of three days or fewer is too short and treated a recess of more than three but fewer than ten days as presumptively too short, allowing for highly unusual circumstances. The Senate also must retain the capacity to transact business for a declared session to count.

conflicts.heading: Informal adjudication still has APA protections
conflicts.body: The matrix describes informal adjudication as outside the APA. It falls outside the APA’s formal hearing provisions. Generally applicable provisions such as §§ 555 and 558 can still apply, alongside the organic statute, agency rules and due process.

conflicts.heading: Section 553(c) and formal rulemaking
conflicts.body: The matrix’s transition from § 553 to §§ 556–557 refers to the route into the formal proceedings. Sections 556–557 replace § 553(c) where triggered. Check any applicable § 553 provisions outside subsection (c) and any additional procedure supplied by the organic statute.

file: Class 14 - Delegating Adjudicative Power - Procedural Due Process  - 10-19- 2026.pptx
title: Delegating adjudicative power and procedural due process

topics.heading: Rulemaking and adjudication under § 551
topics.body: Use the APA’s defined outputs. Rules may have particular applicability and a future effect. Adjudication is the process for producing an order, which can have broader precedential effects. The deck tests the distinction with an FTC complaint affecting other firms, FCC captioning standards for five networks and a loan fee applying across a program.

topics.heading: Ratemaking and licensing cross the intuitive categories
topics.body: The deck’s table separates the statutory classification from the function’s mixed features. The APA treats ratemaking as rulemaking and licensing as adjudication even though licenses authorize future activity and rates can draw on judgments about past costs or practices.

topics.heading: Potential constitutional bases for agency adjudication
topics.body: Start with the nature of the claim. The lecture uses Murray’s Lessee to introduce public rights and describes adjunct fact-finding, integration into a federal regulatory scheme and consent as other historically relevant routes. The slide asking whether court removal might cure a problem is a hypothetical.

topics.heading: Jarkesy’s two questions
topics.body: First ask whether the statutory claim is legal in nature, giving particular weight to the remedy. Then ask whether the public-rights exception permits agency adjudication. Jarkesy involved a fraud analogue and civil penalties serving punishment and deterrence. Atlas Roofing involved statutory obligations without a common-law analogue. The dissent would have allowed adjudication of the government’s statutory enforcement claim.

topics.heading: Liberty, property and the changing public sector
topics.body: The lecture uses Reich’s New Property and Cafeteria Workers to contrast the economic importance of a benefit with the legal basis for claiming it. Cafeteria Workers involved exclusion from a specific military installation, with the employee’s occupation otherwise open to her. Identify the precise interest and effect of the deprivation.

topics.heading: Discretion-limiting terms and the scholarship hypothetical
topics.body: Roth and Perry v. Sindermann distinguish an expectation from an entitlement grounded in an independent source such as a statute, rule or mutually explicit understanding. Compare the scholarship promised after a stated GPA with one that officials may award based on an evaluative judgment. Identify the criteria the claimant can invoke, then use Mathews to decide the procedure.

conflicts.heading: The APA’s formal-adjudication threshold
conflicts.body: The recap’s shorthand about APA coverage concerns §§ 554 and 556–557. The Atlas casebook account also identifies generally applicable APA provisions for informal adjudication.

conflicts.heading: The scope of the due-process requirement
conflicts.body: The deck’s heading about due process and Congress addresses the Londoner–Bi-Metallic individual-hearing distinction. An adjudicative deprivation can require individual process. Congress can impose statutory safeguards on rulemaking and remains subject to independent constitutional constraints.

title: Mathews balancing and statutory hearing rights

topics.heading: The three steps of a due-process analysis
topics.body: Classify the government action under Londoner and Bi-Metallic. Identify the protected deprivation, grounding a claimed property interest in the discretion-limiting law the claimant can invoke. Then apply Mathews to the specific missing safeguard and the time at which it could help.

topics.heading: What extra procedure buys in Mathews
topics.body: Weigh the private interest, error risk and marginal value of another safeguard, and the government’s functional and fiscal interests. The deck contrasts expert assessment of written medical evidence with the claimant’s hardship, and asks who bears uncertainty about whether added procedure improves results.

topics.heading: Loudermill and the timing of a meaningful response
topics.body: The lecture applies Mathews to for-cause public employment. Notice of the charges, an explanation of the employer’s evidence and a chance to respond come before removal, in light of the fuller review available afterward. The apparent clarity of the underlying fact still leaves room to contest significance, intent or appropriate discipline.

topics.heading: Access to evidence and cross-examination are separate safeguards
topics.body: Use the Brock voting table to analyze disclosure of the adverse evidence and cross-examination separately. The controlling middle position required information about the evidence and an opportunity to respond at the preliminary reinstatement stage while allowing cross-examination to await later process.

topics.heading: Three ways statutes lead to a hearing
topics.body: A statute can create a property interest protected by constitutional due process, trigger APA on-the-record procedures, or provide its own form of hearing. The table and hearing images distinguish a legislative-style opportunity to present views from a trial-type process for testing disputed evidence.

topics.heading: Florida East Coast’s construction of the hearing requirement
topics.body: Read the Interstate Commerce Act with the APA. The prospective freight-car proceeding and the 1966 amendment’s substantive factors did not establish an APA on-the-record requirement. The statute’s own hearing requirement allowed written participation on these facts. The deck asks, separately, whether written evidence could also suffice in a proceeding where § 556(d) did apply.

topics.heading: Marathon Oil and the nature of the proceeding
topics.body: The Ninth Circuit treated individual effluent-discharge permits as adjudication and inferred the formal record requirement from the statute’s hearing language and the type of proceeding. Material omitted from the certified record required a remand. The lecture presents this as a contrast with Florida East Coast and flags the division of approaches outside the Ninth Circuit.

topics.heading: Third-party participation and comparative hearings
topics.body: The organic statute or agency rules can permit third parties to seek or join agency hearings. In Ashbacker, granting one of two simultaneous bona fide mutually exclusive applications first would defeat the loser’s statutory hearing. Comparative consideration makes the promised participation meaningful.

conflicts.heading: Loudermill appears in the assigned casebook pages
conflicts.body: The deck labels Loudermill unassigned and marks the full-opinion quotation as outside the casebook. Mashaw p. 487, within the Class 14 assignment, discusses and quotes Loudermill. Retain the distinction between a casebook note, a standalone assigned opinion and the fuller Class 15 lecture treatment.

conflicts.heading: Mathews does not prescribe a universal formal hearing
conflicts.body: The checklist compresses common safeguards and suggests a full hearing for any substantial interest. The governing inquiry is context-specific. Existing procedures, the timing and nature of any later opportunity, and the marginal benefit of a trial-type hearing determine what due process requires.

file: Class 16 - Agency RM and Choice of Procedure 10-26-2026.pptx
title: Agency rulemaking and choice of procedure

topics.heading: Two distinct issues in Marathon Oil
topics.body: The APA record requirement barred reliance on the internal report that never entered the certified record. The regional director could decide this initial licensing matter despite objections based on the agency’s separation of functions and alleged bias. Identify the specific licensing exception and keep the statutory and constitutional objections distinct.

topics.heading: Informal adjudication and hybrid rulemaking
topics.body: Agencies can resolve initial applications, inspections and investigations through informal adjudication, sometimes with tailored procedures and later review. Hybrid rulemaking adds requirements such as a docket or legislative-style hearing to notice and comment. These proceedings can conduct meaningful participation without importing the complete formal hearing framework.

topics.heading: Notice, settlement and separation of functions
topics.body: Sections 554 and 556 address notice, opportunities to settle and who may preside. The classroom ex parte table compares § 554(d)’s safeguard against private consultation on facts in issue with § 557(d)’s bar on relevant merits communications between interested outsiders and decisional personnel. Check the applicable exceptions and scope before applying either provision.

topics.heading: Official notice and the record
topics.body: An agency’s official notice can reach material beyond the usual judicial-notice categories. Section 556(e) protects the party’s opportunity, on timely request, to show the contrary when a noticed material fact outside the evidence supports the decision.

topics.heading: Reliable hearsay under Perales
topics.body: Written reports from examining physicians could constitute substantial evidence in the circumstances of Perales. Distinguish the reports’ reliability and the opportunity to subpoena their authors from the separate question whether a state requires some nonhearsay support under a residuum rule.

topics.heading: The separate stages of § 553
topics.body: Identify proposal notice, public comment, the statement of basis and purpose and the final rule’s effective-date interval. The classroom table distinguishes exclusions from all of § 553, exemptions affecting proposal notice and related comment and exemptions from the 30-day effective-date requirement. A good-cause finding is tied to the requirement the agency seeks to skip.

topics.heading: Same policy issue, different legal instruments
topics.body: The airline stock-sale problem asks whether the second instrument explains an existing transfer restriction or supplies a new operative obligation. The FTC examples compare a binding standard for deceptive advertising, an interpretation of an existing standard, discretionary enforcement guidance and individual adjudications applying the standard.

conflicts.heading: Substantial-evidence review depends on the review provision
conflicts.body: Slide 12’s broad formulation is useful for the hearsay example. In a federal APA problem, § 706(2)(E) applies to proceedings under §§ 556–557 or otherwise reviewed on a statutorily provided hearing record. Identify any applicable organic-statute or state-law review standard separately.

conflicts.heading: Interpretive rules and their underlying law
conflicts.body: The slide calls interpretations binding in a limited sense. The existing statute or legislative rule supplies the binding duty. An interpretive rule can state an agency view of that duty. It needs the corresponding legislative-rule authority and procedures if it imposes a new binding obligation.

file: Class 17 - Choice of Procedure - Notice and Comment - 10-28-2026.pptx
title: Choice of procedure and notice and comment

topics.heading: Policy instruments and the participation tradeoff
topics.body: Compare the slide matrix across three routes. Notice and comment brings wider participation and a record of competing views. An interpretive rule can convey the agency’s view quickly but usually has a thinner testing record. Adjudication develops policy through individual disputes, with formal safeguards for the targeted party where applicable.

topics.heading: Chenery I and II answer different questions
topics.body: Chenery I rejected the SEC’s stated equity-precedent rationale and required the agency to reconsider. Chenery II allowed the SEC to explain the outcome through its statutory policy judgment and develop the principle in adjudication. Compare agency authority to use both modes, the reasons actually given and fairness when imposing an unfamiliar norm.

topics.heading: Rules can resolve general premises of an individual case
topics.body: Heckler v. Campbell, identified as a supplemental case, illustrates the allocation. The Social Security grid resolves recurring vocational questions using categories such as age, education and prior work. The claimant still receives a meaningful hearing on individual characteristics and whether the grid applies to those facts.

topics.heading: Changing an existing rule
topics.body: The APA’s definition of rulemaking includes amending or repealing a rule. Identify the binding existing rule and the procedure needed to amend it. The lecture distinguishes formally changing a rule from deciding an individual case under it, with separate considerations for internal practice rules.

topics.heading: FTC rulemaking authority and noncompetes
topics.body: Petroleum Refiners read §§ 5 and 6(g) of the FTC Act together and treated rulemaking as complementing case-by-case enforcement. The lecture tests a different application in the FTC’s 2024 competition rule, separating the claimed source of competition-rule authority from special statutory procedures for unfair or deceptive practices.

topics.heading: Nova Scotia’s notice and technical record
topics.body: The chart compares the FDA’s original time-temperature-salinity proposal with the final brining alternative and the rejected species-specific approach. The federal enforcement proceeding exposed the scientific studies behind the rule. The Second Circuit held that failing to disclose the relied-on technical basis prevented meaningful participation.

topics.heading: The statement of basis and purpose addresses material objections
topics.body: Nova Scotia identifies unanswered questions about applying one standard across fish species, the suggested lower-temperature alternatives and whether the rule would make whitefish commercially infeasible. A concise explanation still needs to show how the agency addressed significant objections bearing on the adopted rule.

conflicts.heading: Noncompete litigation posture
conflicts.body: Slide 23 compresses two proceedings. The Northern District of Texas set the rule aside in Ryan. The Middle District of Florida granted preliminary relief in Properties of the Villages. In September 2025 the FTC moved to end both appeals and acceded to the Texas vacatur. These were district-court dispositions followed by dismissed appeals.

conflicts.heading: The FTC Act specifies an informal hearing opportunity
conflicts.body: The slide’s shorthand for 15 U.S.C. § 57a refers to the statutory opportunity for an informal hearing and certain procedures for disputed material facts. The unfair-or-deceptive-practices statute does not invoke the ordinary APA formal hearing procedure under §§ 556–557.

conflicts.heading: Public availability alone does not answer Nova Scotia
conflicts.body: The slide lists publicly available data and expertise as possible reasons disclosure might be unnecessary. The opinion held that the agency had to identify the research on which it relied even though pertinent research was readily available. The court recognized that an agency can draw on its own expertise outside the record, but the public still needs enough information about the decisive scientific basis to comment effectively.

file: Class 18 - From Vermont Yankee to Hard Look Review - 11-2-2026.pptx
title: From Vermont Yankee to Hard Look Review

topics.heading: A final rule needs fair notice
topics.body: The logical-outgrowth inquiry asks whether the proposal gave interested people a fair chance to address the approach adopted. Mock contrasts ATF’s proposed point system with its final balancing test. The dissent treated some actual comments as evidence of notice.

topics.heading: Participation depends on usable information
topics.body: Online dockets, advance notices and meetings can make rulemaking more accessible. The class asks who can make informed comments and how agencies can respond effectively when the volume of submissions rises.

topics.heading: Vermont Yankee limits judicial additions to procedure
topics.body: The disputed nuclear-fuel rule used an environmental-impact table. The lecture separates whether the evidence could support the rule from whether a court could require cross-examination beyond the governing procedural law.

topics.heading: Informal proceedings still need a reviewable account
topics.body: The lecture asks whether undisclosed contacts can impair review of rulemaking. It also contrasts the different prejudgment standards used in adjudication and rulemaking and connects meaningful notice with the agency’s final explanation.

topics.heading: Boyd distinguishes an informal record from a formal hearing
topics.body: The Safety Act’s reference to APA procedures and a record for review did not require a trial-type hearing for the factory-installed head-restraint rule. Statutory language, legislative history and the legislative nature of the task all informed the reading.

topics.heading: The basis-and-purpose statement must explain major choices
topics.body: Boyd reads § 553(c) to require enough explanation to identify significant issues and understand the agency’s resolution. A short statement can suffice when the explanation and record show the agency’s reasoning.

topics.heading: Brinegar tests an agency’s evidence against statutory criteria
topics.body: The tire-marking exercise tests the safety benefit and practicability of agency-added labels. The court had to distinguish the lack of factual support for practicability from the agency’s inadequate response to retreaders’ objections.

conflicts.heading: Boyd involved the 1966 Safety Act
conflicts.body: Slide 24 dates the Act to 1968. The Atlas brief correctly dates the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act to 1966 and the Boyd opinion to 1968.

authority.label: National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966

file: Class 19 - Hard Look Review and  553 Exceptions 2- 11-4- 2026.pptx
title: Hard Look Review and § 553 Exceptions

topics.heading: State Farm requires reasons within a narrow scope of review
topics.body: Identify the agency’s own explanation and test it against the record and the criteria Congress supplied. A court may discern an imperfectly stated rationale, but it cannot supply a discretionary judgment the agency never made.

topics.heading: Rescinding a rule requires considering obvious alternatives
topics.body: The passive-restraint rescission omitted an airbag-only option. The Justices also disagreed about whether the agency adequately explained its prediction that drivers would disconnect automatic belts.

topics.heading: Predictive judgments need a reasoned record
topics.body: The diesel-emissions rule turned on development steps and the likelihood of completing them by the compliance deadline. The court assessed whether the agency answered serious objections and explained its forecast.

topics.heading: Vacatur and remand are distinct remedial choices
topics.body: The course compares remand with and without vacatur and asks whether leaving a rule temporarily in effect could undermine prompt correction.

topics.heading: Match a § 553 exception to the duty at issue
topics.body: The lecture distinguishes exemptions from the whole section, exemptions affecting notice and public procedure, and exemptions from advance publication. A claim of good cause must identify the specific statutory ground.

topics.heading: A policy statement leaves room for decision
topics.body: Compare how the agency uses the document with how it labels it. Community Nutrition and General Electric ask whether purported guidance binds field staff, applicants or the decision-maker in practice.

topics.heading: Guidance classification can shape reviewability
topics.body: A claim that guidance effectively establishes a binding rule can raise both notice-and-comment and finality issues. The DAPA example asks what evidence shows that officials actually retain case-by-case discretion.

conflicts.heading: APA § 704 has two routes to review
conflicts.body: Slide 24 describes APA review as available only for final agency action. Section 704 also covers agency action expressly made reviewable by statute. An agency’s policy label does not itself settle the § 704 question.

file: Class 20 - Review under the Arbitrary and Capricious Standard 11-9-26 - 2026.pptx
title: Review under the Arbitrary and Capricious Standard

topics.heading: Locate the existing legal obligation
topics.body: An interpretive rule explains a pre-existing obligation. American Mining Congress asks whether existing law would support enforcement without the new statement, whether the agency invoked legislative authority and whether the statement effectively amended a legislative rule.

topics.heading: An implementation choice can create new law
topics.body: Compare the accessible-sightline examples with Hoctor’s eight-foot fence rule. The closer an instruction follows from existing language, the stronger its claim to be interpretive. A specific requirement chosen among several permissible alternatives can require legislative-rule procedures.

topics.heading: Changing a genuine interpretation and imposing a new rule
topics.body: Perez allows an agency to revise a genuine interpretive rule without notice and comment. The adoption guidance case illustrates the different issue of adding categorical restrictions without a sufficient basis in existing law.

topics.heading: Good cause and alternative publication sequences
topics.body: An agency invoking good cause must explain it when issuing the rule. Direct final and interim final procedures can still invite comments. Little Sisters asks whether an interim notice provided the information and opportunity the APA requires.

topics.heading: Overton Park starts with reviewability and statutory authority
topics.body: Ask first whether governing law supplies a judicial standard and then how that law limits the agency. The parkland statute constrained the Secretary’s assessment of a feasible and prudent alternative more than an open-ended balancing test would.

topics.heading: Review the agency’s actual rationale
topics.body: The class tests the line between explaining a contemporaneous rationale and inventing a new justification in court. Department of Commerce illustrates remand when the stated reason turns out to be pretextual.

conflicts.heading: Substantial evidence can apply under a special review statute
conflicts.body: Slide 28 limits APA § 706(2)(E) to §§ 556–557 proceedings. The provision also applies where an action is otherwise reviewed on the statutory record of an agency hearing.

file: Class 21 - Reviewing Findings of Fact and Interpretations of Law Before Chevron 11-11-2026.pptx
title: Reviewing Findings of Fact and Interpretations of Law Before Chevron

topics.heading: Pacifica left room for later policy disputes
topics.body: Earlier FCC treatment of isolated expletives and the move toward context-sensitive enforcement frame the policy-change question in Fox. Pacifica’s limited holding did not settle every later use or a criminal application.

topics.heading: Fox tests reasons for changing policy
topics.body: The agency must acknowledge the change and give good reasons. Prior factual findings and serious reliance can demand more explanation. The lecture contrasts the Court’s test with Kennedy’s concurrence and Breyer’s dissent.

topics.heading: Regents separates alternatives, reliance and later rationales
topics.body: DHS needed to consider preserving deferred action without associated benefits and to assess serious reliance interests. A later memorandum supplying a new rationale did not cure those omissions.

topics.heading: Substantial evidence means looking at the whole record
topics.body: Universal Camera requires consideration of evidence that cuts against the agency, including the examiner’s credibility assessment. Allentown tests whether the agency’s announced standard was actually applied to the evidence.

topics.heading: ADAPSO distinguishes the available record
topics.body: The D.C. Circuit treated the minimum evidentiary support required for factual findings as equivalent under the two review standards. It distinguished the formal record from other material that was before the agency when it acted.

topics.heading: Mixed questions combine law, fact and application
topics.body: Hearst asks whether the agency may treat news sellers as employees, whether the findings are supported and whether applying the category reasonably serves the statute. The hypothetical makes the distinct inquiries visible.

topics.heading: Skidmore respect comes from persuasive reasoning
topics.body: In the firefighters’ waiting-time case, the agency’s legal position furnished potentially useful guidance. Its thoroughness, reasoning and consistency determined the weight it earned.

topics.heading: The historical Chevron inquiry asked two different questions
topics.body: The stationary-source example separates an independently resolved question at step one from a permissible agency construction at step two. The class compares modest and expansive accounts of how much Chevron changed earlier practice.

conflicts.heading: Regents was a 2020 DHS case
conflicts.body: Slide 16 dates the case to 2015 and refers to HHS. The Supreme Court decided Regents in 2020. The agency was the Department of Homeland Security. The 2015 date belongs to the separate DAPA appellate decision cited in the lecture.

conflicts.heading: The Fox standard was part of the Court’s opinion
conflicts.body: Slides 10 and 11 call the relevant reasoning a plurality. Scalia wrote for the Court on the ordinary policy-change standard and its principal application. Only Part III-E lacked a majority.

topics.heading: Chevron and hard look review addressed different questions
topics.body: The lecture reviews Chevron’s historical two steps and arguments for and against deference, then separately identifies why a policy choice or factual judgment can fail reasoned-decisionmaking review.

topics.heading: Mead’s historical threshold asked about force of law
topics.body: Chevron eligibility turned on whether Congress delegated force-of-law authority and whether the agency acted through it. The customs letters applied to particular transactions and were issued in great numbers without ordinary public procedure.

topics.heading: Skidmore asks what makes an interpretation persuasive
topics.body: The lecture tests thoroughness, quality of reasoning, consistency, expertise and the nature of public input. The agency can earn weight even when the form of its interpretation does not qualify for historical Chevron treatment.

topics.heading: King illustrates an extraordinary issue under Chevron
topics.body: The Court independently decided whether ACA tax credits reached federal exchanges because of the issue’s significance, its centrality to the scheme and the mismatch with IRS expertise. The class compares possible applications to other agency disputes.

topics.heading: Apply Loper Bright to the question actually presented
topics.body: The fisheries statute permits observer requirements and expressly allocates costs for some groups. The dispute concerned whether other vessel owners could be required to pay. The Supreme Court set the standard of review and remanded the observer-payment cases.

topics.heading: Independent judgment preserves actual delegated choices
topics.body: Courts independently identify the best statutory reading and the boundaries of any delegation. Within those bounds the agency exercises the delegated discretion and supplies a reasoned explanation. Statutory ambiguity alone no longer triggers Chevron.

topics.heading: Prior statutory holdings and historical interpretations
topics.body: The Court distinguished rejecting Chevron’s method from reopening holdings on particular agency actions. The lecture compares majority and dissent accounts of earlier practice, workability and reliance.

topics.heading: Why study contract law
topics.body: Slide 4 gives the reasons: contracts are everywhere, contract law often trumps, it has economic, moral and political significance, and it brings professional benefits. The four values it lists are autonomy, efficiency, fairness and distributive justice. Slide 5 quotes Vonnegut on transactional lawyers, and Slide 6 says the course teaches how to litigate contractual disputes and how to draft contracts.

topics.heading: Four questions and the map of the course
topics.body: Every problem is organized by four questions: is there an enforceable promise, has it been breached, has performance been excused, and how should the promise be enforced. Slide 8 groups the course into formation, validity, interpretation, excuses and remedies, and lists related causes of action: promissory estoppel, restitution, misrepresentation, tortious interference and negligence.

topics.heading: Sources of US contract law and where disputes are decided
topics.body: Slide 9 lists treaties (for example the CISG), federal legislation and common law, state legislation (UCC Article 2, the New York General Obligations Law) and state common law, which is non-uniform, includes equity and is synthesized in the Restatement (Second) of Contracts. Disputes are decided in federal court, state court (noting the possibility of a jury) or arbitration.

topics.heading: The Apple App Store licence as a first contract
topics.body: Slide 10 gives the App Store's scale: about 2 million apps, “$1.3 trillion in billings and sales” in 2024, and 97.7% of apps using the default licence. Slide 11 applies the four questions to a developer who fails to perform and to a user who fails to perform, and asks which procedural rules would govern a suit and where the adjudicator would find the legal rules.

topics.heading: Hawkins v. McGee
topics.body: The slides ask what happened, whether there was an enforceable promise and why, whether it was breached and how it should be enforced. Slide 13 quotes the two statements at issue: “Three or four days, not over four...” and “I will guarantee to make the hand a hundred per cent perfect hand or a hundred per cent good hand.” Slide 14 sets out three positions to compare: operation pain with a perfect hand, a scarred hand, and operation pain with a hairy hand.

topics.heading: Bayliner Marine Corp. v. Crow and implied merchantability
topics.body: The slides ask whether there was an enforceable promise and which rules the court applied, then vary the facts: a salesperson who says “in my opinion, this boat will go 30 miles per hour, no trouble”, and a boat with no speed statement whose maximum speed is two miles per hour. Slide 17 quotes UCC § 2-314 on the implied warranty of merchantability.

topics.heading: Problem for next class
topics.body: Slide 18 assigns the Applying the Interests problem at p. 18.

topics.heading: How should the promise be enforced?
topics.body: The class covers alternative measures of damages, expectation damages as the default measure, specific relief and efficient breach. Slide 4 breaks the fourth key question into damages (and which measure), specific performance and imprisonment.

topics.heading: Possible measures of damages
topics.body: Slide 5's table pairs each measure with the party it looks at and the baseline it restores: restitution looks at the promisor as if the contract had never been made, to the extent of benefits received from the promisee; reliance and expectation look at the promisee as if the contract had never been made or had been performed; disgorgement looks at the promisor as if it had been performed. Punitive damages are listed with no entry.

topics.heading: Sullivan v. O’Connor
topics.body: The slides ask what the basis of the claim was, what promise was enforced, the policy arguments for and against enforcement, and which measure of damages the court favoured and why. Slide 7 quotes the court on doctors seldom being able to promise specific results in good faith, the risk of “defensive medicine”, and the opposite fear of exposing the public to charlatans.

topics.heading: Applying the Interests: the figures
topics.body: The problem's figures are a $300 doctor's fee, a $100 hospital fee and $3,000 of pain per operation, a $20,000 promised benefit and $10,000 of disfigurement. The table totals the position if the contract was performed at $13,500 and if it was breached at −$19,600; Slide 10 adds a contract never made with a lost opportunity, also $13,500. The restitution, reliance and expectation amounts are left blank for the class to fill in.

topics.heading: When specific performance is available
topics.body: Slide 11 says specific performance is traditionally available when the remedy at law is inadequate (or, under the UCC, “where the goods are unique or in other proper circumstances”), with inadequacy presumed for sales of land; when equitable relief is appropriate (no unclean hands, a contract that is not unfair, no laches, security for the promisor's performance, enforcement not impractical); and when the contract is not one for personal services.

topics.heading: Morris v. Sparrow
topics.body: The questions are whether the contract was breached, whether performance was excused and why damages were inadequate. The slide then asks what would follow if Sparrow intended to sell Keno, whether a buyer from Sparrow would get specific performance, and whether Sparrow would have any incentive, after breach but before trial, to buy another roping horse.

topics.heading: US Naval Institute and efficient breach
topics.body: Slide 13 asks about the applicable law, the promise, the breach, the damages awarded at trial and on appeal, and why the amount was uncertain. Slide 14 assumes profits from breach above $100,000 and damages below $40,000 and asks whether this is an efficient breach, defined as “one that leaves the promisor better off and the promisee no worse off”, and whether you would advise Berkley to breach. Slide 15 quotes New York Rules of Professional Conduct 1.2(d) and 2.1. The slides state no conclusion.

topics.heading: White v. Benkowski
topics.body: The slide asks for the measure of expectation damages and of punitive damages, why the jury awarded punitive damages, why the Supreme Court disallowed them, and how the Whites could have avoided this outcome. Slide 17 assigns the Discounting Retirement problem at p. 59 for the next class.

topics.heading: Recap: the four questions and the first cases
topics.body: Slide 3 files the first cases under the key questions: an enforceable promise (Hawkins, Sullivan), breach (Bayliner, US Naval Institute), excuse (Morris) and enforcement (Hawkins, Sullivan, Morris, White). Slides 4 and 5 repeat the Class 2 efficient-breach question about US Naval Institute and the New York professional conduct rules.

topics.heading: Requirements for formation and enforceability
topics.body: Formation requires offer and acceptance or mutual assent, consideration and definiteness. Formalities are prerequisites to enforceability for some contracts. Statutes sometimes permit formation without consideration, usually with formalities. Promises without consideration may be enforced through promissory estoppel, and may lead to liability in tort or restitution.

topics.heading: What consideration is
topics.body: Consideration is a performance or return promise “bargained for” by the promisor; performance includes an act, a forbearance and the alteration of legal rights. Something is bargained for if it appears to be sought by the promisor and induced by the promise. Adequacy is arguably irrelevant: equivalence is not required, but some courts have held nominal consideration insufficient. The speaker note cites Restatement §§ 71, 79 and 81.

topics.heading: When the requirement of consideration matters
topics.body: A promise lacks consideration when nothing is given in return (intra-familial gifts, charitable subscriptions, firm offers, contract modifications and, arguably, compromises and illusory promises) or when what is given was not sought or not induced (past consideration, and rewards unknown to the promisee, which are also analysed as failures of assent). Slide 12 marks in bold, as possibly enforceable under the New York General Obligations Law, firm offers, contract modifications, past consideration and rewards.

topics.heading: Hamer v. Sidway
topics.body: The slide asks who Hamer and Sidway were, what the purported consideration for the uncle's promise was, whether the uncle could have sued had he found his nephew drinking at 18, what the court concluded and what a modern court would conclude, and the arguments for and against enforcing the uncle's promise and intra-familial promises generally.

topics.heading: Why require consideration?
topics.body: Slide 14 asks whether consideration ensures that a transaction is efficient or fair, or serves as a useful formality: does it provide evidence that a promise was made, induce caution, or evidence an intention to be legally bound?

topics.heading: Dyer v. National By-Products
topics.body: The slide asks what promise Dyer sought to enforce, what the purported consideration was, whether it fits the conventional definition, and what rule the court used. It varies the facts (Dyer always knew the claim was invalid; Dyer would have sued anyway) and asks whether courts should enforce settlements of bad-faith claims.

topics.heading: Problem: Discounting Retirement
topics.body: Hurley promises Marine not to compete for x years; the Employee Retirement Plan and Trust Fund pays Hurley's vested share immediately instead of after the five-year waiting period; Hurley breaches the non-competition agreement. The slide asks whether Marine can sue for breach of contract.

topics.heading: Formalities: examples, functions and concerns
topics.body: Slide 18 lists writing, seal, notarization and, with a question mark, consideration as formalities. Slide 19 gives their evidentiary, cautionary and channeling functions, and two concerns: cost and prejudice to unsophisticated parties.

topics.heading: The Statute of Frauds
topics.body: Slide 20's non-exhaustive list covers contracts binding executors and administrators, to answer for another's debt, upon consideration of marriage, for an interest in land, not to be performed within one year, and for goods over $500 (UCC § 2-201; compare CISG Art. 11). Exceptions include part performance, estoppel and reliance, merchant confirmations not objected to within ten days, judicial admissions and qualified financial contracts. A sufficient writing is signed and contains the essential terms, though § 2-201(1) asks only that it indicate a contract for sale; electronic records and signatures qualify.

topics.heading: Tolosa v. HSBC
topics.body: The slide asks what promise the plaintiffs sought to enforce, whether it was within the Statute of Frauds and satisfied it, whether any exception applied, and what policy justifies refusing enforcement. Slide 24 quotes Texas Business and Commerce Code § 26.02(e), which requires a conspicuous notice that the written loan agreement is final and that there are no unwritten oral agreements.

topics.heading: The Dr. Dre prenuptial agreement
topics.body: The slides take a news report that Nicole Young claimed she signed a prenup in 1996 under pressure and that Dr. Dre later tore it up. They ask what legal effect Young gave the gesture, the policy arguments for and against her position and his likely defence, and quote California Family Code §§ 1611 and 1614: a premarital agreement must be written and signed by both parties, and after marriage may be amended or revoked only by a signed writing; both are enforceable without consideration.

topics.heading: Problem for next class
topics.body: Slide 27 assigns This Contract Is Toast at p. 111.

topics.heading: Conditions
topics.body: The class covers conditions, illusory promises, satisfaction clauses, exclusive dealing, requirements and output contracts, the implied duty of good faith, UCC § 2-306, and mandatory versus default rules. Slide 4 quotes Restatement § 224: a condition is “an event, not certain to occur, which must occur, unless its nonoccurrence is excused, before performance under a contract becomes due”, and points to the note on conditional promises at p. 96.

topics.heading: Mattei v. Hopper and satisfaction clauses
topics.body: The condition was “subject to Coldwell Banker & Co. obtaining leases satisfactory to the purchaser.” Slide 5 offers three readings (absolute discretion, satisfactory to a reasonable person, a determination made in good faith) and asks why the court went beyond the plain language, whether the parties would have wanted that reading, and whether one can contract around it. Slide 6 shows drafting that does: “acting at his sole discretion”, with a definition excluding any standard of reasonableness.

topics.heading: Wood v. Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon
topics.body: Slide 7 quotes the agreement: Wood's exclusive right to place endorsements, the equal division of profits and the monthly accounting. Slide 8 asks what Lucy promised, what consideration Wood provided, and whether the court read Wood's obligations as none, reasonable efforts or best efforts, then asks why the court went beyond the express terms and whether the parties could contract around it.

topics.heading: UCC § 2-306: exclusive dealing, output and requirements
topics.body: Section 2-306(2) imposes, unless otherwise agreed, best efforts to supply and to promote sales under a lawful exclusive-dealing agreement; the slide notes that Comment 5 speaks of reasonable diligence, reasonable effort and due diligence. Section 2-306(1) measures output or requirements by what occurs in good faith, without quantities unreasonably disproportionate to an estimate or to prior output or requirements. The commentary allows reasonable elasticity, a shutdown “for lack of orders” but not “merely to curtail losses”, and “normal” but not “sudden” expansion. The slide asks what follows if a buyer says its requirements are zero or increases them dramatically.

topics.heading: Structural Polymer Group v. Zoltek
topics.body: The slide asks about the applicable law, the seller's promise and the return promise, how and why the court interpreted it, whether the parties could contract around that reading, and how damages were calculated. Slide 11 lists yearly quantities without units: 28,219 and 20,943 (PANEX 33) in 2000 and 2001, 1,763 returned in 2002, none in 2003, then 548,935, 1,480,138 and 2,480,138 (PANEX 35) in 2004 to 2006, the last two marked “not filled”.

topics.heading: Good faith cannot be disclaimed
topics.body: Slide 13 quotes UCC § 1-302(b): the obligations of good faith, diligence, reasonableness and care cannot be disclaimed by agreement, but the parties may set standards for measuring them that are not manifestly unreasonable, and may fix a time for action that is not manifestly unreasonable.

topics.heading: Summary: reading in obligations to find consideration
topics.body: Courts may read agreements in which one party makes only illusory promises, or none, as imposing more robust obligations (for example good faith) that count as consideration. It is unclear whether they do so to make the agreement enforceable or because the reading matches the parties' intentions, fairness or efficiency. If it does not match the parties' intentions, the slide lists three concerns: incentives for inefficient behaviour, uncertainty and costly litigation, and incentives to invest in drafting.

topics.heading: Problem: This Contract Is Toast
topics.body: The slide asks whether there is a contract, whether Staehl Bread has breached, what the damages are, and how Walker could have drafted the contract to protect itself.

topics.heading: Overview of restitution
topics.body: Restitution is a broad term for recovery based on unjust enrichment. It is commonly awarded for mistaken payments, implied contracts, contracts avoided for misrepresentation, and contracts whose performance is excused by breach, impossibility or non-occurrence of a condition. Recovery may be measured by the cost of the goods or services or by how far they increased the value of the defendant's property or advanced the defendant's interests. Legal qualification: restitution measures the benefit the defendant received, not the claimant's loss (C&M 145); under Restatement (Second) § 371(a) the cost is what it would have cost the defendant to obtain the benefit from someone in the claimant's position, and “implied contracts” in this list is best read as contracts implied in law (quasi-contract), a claim for unjust enrichment rather than on a true contract (C&M 146).

topics.heading: History and uses of promissory estoppel
topics.body: Promissory estoppel is an equitable doctrine developed from equitable estoppel, which precludes denial of facts; promissory estoppel precludes denial of a binding promise. It is endorsed in Restatement (Second) §§ 87–90, led Gilmore to predict “The Death of Contract”, and is frequently argued but often without success. Slide 5 lists its applications: promises to family members, gifts to charity, firm offers, modifications, promises to employees and preliminary negotiations.

topics.heading: The elements in Restatement § 90
topics.body: Section 90(1) makes binding a promise the promisor should reasonably expect to induce action or forbearance, which does induce it, if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement; the remedy may be limited as justice requires. Comment b calls the principle flexible and lists factors bearing on injustice, including the reasonableness of the reliance and its definite and substantial character in relation to the remedy sought, the formality of the promise and the policies of enforcing bargains and preventing unjust enrichment. Section 90(2) makes a charitable subscription or marriage settlement binding under Subsection (1) without proof that the promise induced action or forbearance. Legal qualification: the casebook reports that the law on charitable subscriptions remains unsettled and that most jurisdictions have not addressed it; Massachusetts in King v. Trustees of Boston University still required consideration or reliance (C&M 129).

topics.heading: Contract and promissory estoppel compared
topics.body: Slide 9 lists three possible differences: the requirement of consideration, whether a definite promise is required, and the remedy. The last two carry question marks. Legal qualification: § 90’s black letter does not say the promise must be definite, though Minnesota in Cohen required a “clear and definite” one (C&M 135); § 90(1) allows the remedy to be limited as justice requires, but comment d says full-scale enforcement is often appropriate, as in Ricketts and Feinberg (C&M 123, 128).

topics.heading: Ricketts v. Scothorn
topics.body: Slide 10 quotes the note (“I promise to pay Katie Scothorn on demand, $2,000 to be at 6 per cent per annum”) and the grandfather's statement that none of his grandchildren work and she need not. Slide 11 asks whether there was a contract, whether the elements of promissory estoppel were present and what remedy was appropriate, then varies the facts: quitting work not mentioned, reliance by buying a horse, and both parties understanding the doctrine of consideration.

topics.heading: Employment at will
topics.body: Slide 14 quotes the at-will rule (either side may end a pure at-will relationship at any time and for any reason without liability; the slide gives no source) and lists, depending on the state, where it may not apply: contracts for a definite term, collective agreements, and terminations that violate public policy, implied terms or the implied duty of good faith. Legal qualification: the power to end the relationship without liability does not end the analysis when a specific assurance induced reliance; in D&G Stout the Seventh Circuit held that, under Indiana law, an assurance within an at-will distributorship could support reliance damages, though not expected future profits (C&M 140–142).

topics.heading: Feinberg v. Pfeiffer Co.
topics.body: Slide 15 lists four candidates for the consideration for the pension promise (past services, a promise to continue in employment, continuation of employment, retirement) beside objections such as “not induced by promise”, “not supported by evidence” and “not sought by promisor”; read in slide order, the objections pair one to one with the candidates (past services, not induced by promise; promise to continue, not supported by evidence; continuation of employment, not sought by promisor and not clearly induced by promise; retirement, not sought by promisor), an inference from the extracted text that matches the casebook (C&M 70, 72). Slide 16 walks through the promissory estoppel elements and varies the facts: she could return to work, she retired for illness, both understood consideration. Slide 17 asks the class to improve the board resolution's drafting.

topics.heading: Cohen v. Cowles Media
topics.body: Slide 18 quotes Justice White: “it is no more than the incidental, and constitutionally insignificant, consequence of applying to the press a generally applicable law that requires those who make certain kinds of promises to keep them.” It asks whether there was consideration and whether each element of promissory estoppel was present. Legal qualification: on remand the Minnesota court required a clear and definite promise, reliance the promisor intended and that was to the promisee’s detriment, and enforcement required to prevent an injustice, a legal question for the court and not whether enforcement would do justice (C&M 135–136).

topics.heading: D&G Stout v. Bacardi Imports
topics.body: The slide asks what the promise was and whether it was broken, whether reliance was reasonable to expect, what the reliance was, whether enforcement was necessary to prevent injustice, what remedy the court would provide, and whether those are expectation or reliance damages. Legal qualification: the Seventh Circuit classified the drop in the sale price as reliance injury, because Bacardi’s withdrawal destroyed an opportunity General already had (C&M 142); the casebook’s note 2 asks whether the remand award resembles the lost-opportunity damages denied elsewhere (C&M 143).

topics.heading: Justifications for consideration and for promissory estoppel
topics.body: Both slides list the key policy considerations of autonomy, efficiency, fairness and distributive justice. Slide 20 asks whether consideration provides evidence of the promise, indicates caution and intention to be bound, or ensures fairness. Slide 21 asks why foreseeable reliance substitutes for consideration, adding whether it ensures fairness by protecting promisees who behave reasonably from detrimental reliance.

conflicts.heading: The Cohen v. Cowles Media citation on slide 18
conflicts.body: The slide cites the quotation as “50 U.S. 663, 672”. The Atlas's Cohen v. Cowles Media entry reports the Supreme Court decision at 501 U.S. 663 (1991). The Class 6 deck (Slide 6) repeats the same citation.

topics.heading: Balfour v. Balfour and intent to be legally bound
topics.body: The class covers intent to be legally bound, alternatives to legal enforcement, the pros and cons of enforceability, and objective and subjective standards of assent. Slide 4 asks what the promise was, whether there was consideration, what other factors the court considered, whether the parties intended a contract, what the effects of unenforceable promises are, what the pros and cons of legally enforceable promises are, and how the parties could have avoided this result.

topics.heading: Restatement § 21: intention to be legally bound
topics.body: Slide 5 quotes § 21: neither real nor apparent intention that a promise be legally binding is essential, but a manifestation of intention that it shall not affect legal relations may prevent formation. Comment c says that for social engagements and agreements within a family the normal understanding is that no legal obligation arises, and some unusual manifestation of intention is necessary to create a contract.

topics.heading: Cohen v. Cowles Media revisited
topics.body: Slide 6 repeats Justice White's “generally applicable law” passage and asks whether the elements of a contract were present, whether the elements of promissory estoppel were present, and whether different answers to the two questions can be justified. Legal qualification: Justice White's sentence comes from the U.S. Supreme Court's 1991 decision reversing the Minnesota court (501 U.S. 663; the slide prints "50 U.S."). The contract question this class reads is the Minnesota Supreme Court's 1990 holding that the reporters' promise was not a contract because the parties did not intend a legally binding one (C&M 183–185).

topics.heading: Lucy v. Zehmer
topics.body: The slide asks what Lucy had to prove, whether Zehmer's drinking was relevant, and what test the court used for mutual assent, varying the facts: Zehmer did not intend to sell; Lucy knew that; Lucy did not know but should have known. It asks which factors made Lucy's belief that Zehmer intended to sell reasonable.

topics.heading: Why an objective standard
topics.body: Slide 9 gives the justifications: autonomy (it “imposes liability on those who knowingly invoke a convention”), efficiency (incentives for speakers to avoid misunderstandings, and avoiding the litigation cost of ascertaining beliefs) and fairness (it “imposes costs on party at fault”). It asks why the law does not require more formalities.

topics.heading: Leonard v. Pepsico and factors under the objective standard
topics.body: Slide 10 introduces Leonard v. Pepsico by name only. Slide 11 lists the factors relevant to the objective standard: language, formality, definiteness or completeness, reasonableness of terms, foreseeable reliance or part performance, conspicuousness, custom, the parties' self-interest and course of dealing.

topics.heading: Specht v. Netscape
topics.body: The slide asks what promise Netscape wanted to enforce, how the plaintiffs allegedly manifested assent, why that was not assent, to which terms (if any) they assented, how Netscape would respond, and whether that response would guarantee “informed assent”.

topics.heading: The Uber sign-up screens
topics.body: Slides 13 to 15 show sign-up screens from Cullinane v. Uber Technologies, 893 F.3d 53 (2018), where “Done” appears once payment information is entered, and Meyer v. Uber Technologies, 868 F.3d 66 (2d Cir. 2017), marked as applying California law. The screens themselves are images whose content is not in the slide text. Legal qualification: Cullinane is a First Circuit decision holding that Uber's registration process did not form a contract because it did not give users reasonable notice of the terms and conditions (as reported in Kauders v. Uber Technologies, C&M 305).

topics.heading: Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 2
topics.body: Slide 16 quotes § 2(a): a standard term is adopted if the consumer manifests assent to the transaction after reasonable notice of the term and of the intent to include it, and a reasonable opportunity to review it. The quoted comment (Comment 3 of the 2024 Official Text; the sentence is not in the Selections' excerpt of the 2019 draft) says the section does not address formation or assent to nonstandard terms; once a contract is formed, it determines which standard terms are adopted. Legal qualification: the slide's black letter matches the 2019 Tentative Draft printed in the Selections (p. 477), which does not say who must prove adoption; the 2024 Official Text begins "if the business demonstrates that the consumer manifested assent," which puts that burden on the business. Subsection (c), also assigned, keeps the contract even if some standard terms are not adopted: its terms are the adopted terms and, if the consumer elects, the unadopted standard terms, with terms supplied by law (the 2024 text adds terms both parties agreed to and terms incorporated by law).

topics.heading: What is an offer?
topics.body: Slide 4 quotes Restatement § 24: an offer is the manifestation of willingness to enter into a bargain so made as to justify another in understanding that assent is invited and will conclude it. Courts routinely distinguish quotes and “invitations to treat” from offers (citing Leonard v. Pepsico), and statements that are not offers may still be tortious or violate consumer protection statutes. The class weighs the rules against the parties' intentions (allowing for judicial error), communication costs, litigation costs and fairness.

topics.heading: Lefkowitz v. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store
topics.body: The slide asks why advertisements are not usually treated as offers, whether it is reasonable to rely on them, whether these advertisements were offers and why, whether the offers were accepted, and how Great Minneapolis would respond.

topics.heading: What constitutes acceptance
topics.body: An acceptance is a manifestation of assent to the offer's terms; the offeror is “master of the offer” and may define what qualifies. Acceptance must be on the same terms and unconditional, may be by promise or by performance, and silence ordinarily is not acceptance. It is effective on dispatch by reasonable means (except for options), and notification of acceptance by promise is ordinarily required.

topics.heading: Notifying acceptance by performance: Restatement § 54
topics.body: Under § 54(1), when an offer invites acceptance by performance, no notification is needed unless the offer requests it. Under § 54(2), if the offeree has reason to know the offeror cannot learn of the performance promptly and with certainty, the offeror's duty is discharged unless the offeree uses reasonable diligence to notify, the offeror learns of it within a reasonable time, or the offer says notification is not required.

topics.heading: Termination of the power of acceptance
topics.body: The power of acceptance ends by lapse (after a reasonable time if the offer sets no period), revocation, rejection or counter-offer, or the offeror's death or supervening incapacity. The slide notes that the last three may not terminate the power to accept an irrevocable offer.

topics.heading: Wucherpfennig v. Dooley
topics.body: The slide sets out the correspondence: on Jan. 4 an offer to sell to Donald “for $200 an acre, provided it is a cash deal & handled promptly”; Jan. 13, Donald “interested”; Feb. 17, “we are therefore ready to proceed with this transaction”, asking the exact amount expected; March 9, revocation. It asks whether the first letter was an offer and whether the Feb. 17 letter was an acceptance.

topics.heading: Problem: Awesome Acceptance?
topics.body: The slide quotes the instant messages: “We can do 2000 orders/day by Friday if I have your blessing”, then “NO LIMIT” and “awesome!”. It asks what the offer was, whether there was an acceptance, and whether it should be possible to modify a contract by instant message.

topics.heading: International Filter Co. v. Conroe Gin, Ice & Light
topics.body: The proposal became “a contract when accepted by the purchaser and approved by an executive officer of the International Filter company” and was “submitted for prompt acceptance”. The slide asks who the offeror was, what constituted acceptance and why that form, whether notification was required and provided, and whether the letter alone would qualify as acceptance.

topics.heading: White v. Corlies & Tift
topics.body: The slide lists the sequence (specifications, estimate, changed specifications, signed revised estimate, note, beginning of performance, countermand) and quotes the note: “Upon an agreement to finish the fitting up of offices 57 Broadway in two weeks from date, you can begin at once.” It asks what the offer was, what sort of acceptance was sought, and whether the offeror dispensed with notification.

topics.heading: Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball
topics.body: Slide 15 quotes the advertisement promising a £100 reward to anyone who caught influenza after using the ball three times daily for two weeks, and the £1000 deposited with the Alliance Bank “shewing our sincerity”. It asks whether the advertisement was an offer, whether it could be revoked before Mrs. Carlill gave notice, after she bought the ball but before using it, or before she caught influenza, and what the consideration was. Slide 14 is an image with no text.
