title: Firm offers and formation under Article 2

topics.heading: Limits on the power of revocation
topics.body: A promise to hold an offer open is enforceable if supported by consideration, made enforceable by statute (UCC § 2-205 or N.Y. Gen. Oblig. L. § 5-1109), or written and signed, reciting a purported consideration and proposing a fair exchange within a reasonable time (Restatement § 87(1)); the Restatement calls this an option contract (§ 25). An offer also becomes irrevocable when it seeks acceptance by performance and the offeree tenders or begins performance (§§ 45, 62), or when it has been relied on (§ 87(2)).

topics.heading: Problem: The Move to Maine
topics.body: The slide compares two versions of the promise: “If you move to Maine and take care of me for the rest of my life you will have the place when I have passed away” and “If you will agree to move to Lewiston and care for me...”. It asks whether there is a contract, and what follows if the offeror died after the offerees sold their home and business but before they moved.

topics.heading: Acceptance by performance and the smoke ball
topics.body: Slides 7 and 9 repeat from Class 7 Restatement § 54 on notifying acceptance by performance and the Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball advertisement and questions about revocation and consideration. Slide 8 is an image with no text.

topics.heading: Drennan v. Star Paving
topics.body: The slide asks what the offer was, whether anything showed it was irrevocable, what form of acceptance was sought, whether Drennan did anything that could be acceptance before revocation, and whether Drennan relied. It asks how the case would be resolved in New York, how the court justified making the offer irrevocable, and why a bidder might be reluctant to make an irrevocable offer and what the court did about that concern.

topics.heading: Battle of the forms at common law
topics.body: Slide 12's table reads two exchanges of forms followed by performance: an invitation to treat, then an offer, accepted by performance; or an offer, then a reply that is a rejection and counter-offer if it does not exactly mirror the offer, accepted by performance.

topics.heading: UCC §§ 2-204 and 2-207
topics.body: Section 2-204 allows a contract for sale in any manner sufficient to show agreement, including conduct, even if the moment of making is undetermined. Section 2-207(1) makes a definite and seasonable expression of acceptance an acceptance even if it adds or changes terms, unless expressly conditional on assent to them; (3) lets conduct recognizing a contract establish one. Under (2), additional terms are proposals that between merchants become part of the contract unless the offer limits acceptance, they materially alter it, or objection is given; under (3) the terms are those on which the writings agree plus supplementary terms.

topics.heading: The § 2-207 table
topics.body: Slide 16 charts the outcomes when an offer meets a second form: a rejection or counter-offer if the reply is not a definite or seasonable acceptance or is expressly conditional, which leads to § 2-207(3); an acceptance whose terms are not incorporated (not between merchants, offer limits acceptance, material alteration, objection, or different terms under the minority rule “consistent with statutory text”); the majority “knockout” rule for different terms; and the “California” rule, implied by Comment 3, incorporating them. Slide 17 applies the same grid to confirmations of an agreement already made.

topics.heading: Dorton v. Collins & Aikman
topics.body: Slide 18 quotes the acknowledgment form making the order subject to all its terms, including arbitration and exclusion of warranties, and listing when it becomes a contract. Slides 19 to 22 apply the § 2-207 table to the order, the acknowledgment “subject to” an arbitration clause and delivery, for the District Court and the Sixth Circuit, and treat a prior oral agreement as a confirmation case. How each court read the table is shown by highlighting that is not in the slide text.

topics.heading: C. Itoh v. Jordan International
topics.body: Slide 23 applies the § 2-207 table to a purchase order, an acceptance “expressly conditional on Buyer’s assent to” an arbitration clause, and delivery and payment.

topics.heading: Bayway and material alteration
topics.body: Slide 24 quotes Comment 4: a material alteration is one that “would result in surprise or hardship if incorporated without express awareness by the other party”, and notes the examples in Comments 4 and 5 and the relevance of trade usage, custom and practice. It asks who bears the burden of proving material alteration, why the tax clause was not one, and whether an arbitration clause necessarily is.

topics.heading: Northrop v. Litronic
topics.body: Slides 25 and 26 apply the § 2-207 table to an offer with a 90-day warranty, an invoice with an unlimited warranty, and delivery, the second for the Seventh Circuit.

topics.heading: Problem: Misplaced Strategies
topics.body: The buyer's purchase order, which has an arbitration clause, says it is the entire agreement notwithstanding any seller's form and cannot be modified except by a writing signed by the buyer. The seller's invoice, silent on arbitration, says it is not an expression of acceptance or confirmation under § 2-207 and that acceptance is expressly conditioned on the buyer's assent to its terms. Slides 28 and 29 return to the table to consider the offeror's and the offeree's strategies.

topics.heading: Policy considerations for the forms rules
topics.body: Rules can be evaluated for respect for the parties' intention, fairness, certainty, litigation costs and drafting costs, and for how they affect incentives to negotiate master agreements, draft clear and reasonable forms, and litigate.

topics.heading: Klocek v. Gateway
topics.body: The class compares approaches to incorporating terms that follow payment and asks whether they ensure meaningful assent and whether that is essential. On Klocek the slide asks what the relevant manifestations of assent were, whether § 2-207 applied, when the contract was formed, which terms were incorporated, and how Gateway could have ensured incorporation and whether that would have ensured meaningful assent.

topics.heading: Hill v. Gateway
topics.body: The slide asks whether § 2-207 applied, what Easterbrook found to be the offer and acceptance and which terms were incorporated, and how the ruling departs from Klocek. It then asks what follows if the seller reneges after payment but before shipping, if the buyer does not know terms will follow, or if return is costly, how the buyers could have avoided incorporation, and why Easterbrook favours incorporating terms that follow.

topics.heading: Pros and cons of Easterbrook’s approach
topics.body: The pros listed are lower costs at the time of the initial transaction and ousting potentially undesirable default terms (UCC gap-fillers). The cons are uncertainty whether the seller is bound before the review period ends, and an incentive for sellers to withhold objectionable terms in the hope that buyers will not see them or return the goods, so that buyers may be bound by terms they would not have agreed to, which may be objectively unfair or welfare-reducing.

topics.heading: An empirical study of pay now, terms later licences
topics.body: Slide 7 reports Marotta-Wurgler, 38 J. Legal Stud. 309 (2009): of 515 end user licence agreements for software sold online, 52% were pay now, terms later. Measured against Article 2 default rules, those licences were not worse for buyers and on average were slightly better.

topics.heading: Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 2(b)
topics.body: Comment 3 (2024 Official Text; Comment 1 in the Selections' 2019 draft) says assent to the transaction usually adopts at least the core deal terms, and other standard terms may be adopted separately. Under § 2(b), a term available only after assent is adopted if the consumer first gets reasonable notice that it will follow, of the chance to review and terminate, and that not terminating adopts it; then gets a reasonable opportunity to review; and then has a reasonable opportunity to terminate without unreasonable cost, loss of value or burden, and does not.

file: Class 10_Precontractual liability, Preliminary agreements and Definiteness - Copy (1).pptx
title: Precontractual liability and definiteness

topics.heading: The requirement of definiteness
topics.body: Slide 5 gives two formulations: terms must “provide a basis for determining the existence of a breach and for giving an appropriate remedy”, or the parties “must have reached agreement on all essential terms.” It adds that damages are not recoverable beyond what the evidence establishes with reasonable certainty, and that specific relief requires sufficiently certain terms. Slide 3 lists definiteness with mutual assent and consideration under the question whether there is an enforceable promise.

topics.heading: Sun Printing & Publishing v. Remington Paper & Power
topics.body: Slide 6 quotes the price clause: price and term to be agreed fifteen days before each period ends, “in no event to be higher than” the Canadian Export Paper Company's contract price to large consumers. Slide 7 asks whether the parties intended to be bound, in what sense the agreement was indefinite, why the court did not fill the gap with reasonable terms, how damages would be calculated, and what if the price had fallen.

topics.heading: Oglebay Norton v. Armco
topics.body: Slide 8 quotes the rate clause: the regular net contract rates recognized by leading iron ore shippers, or, failing those, a rate the parties shall mutually agree considering the leading independent vessel operators' rates. The slides ask what Oglebay sought to enforce, whether the parties intended to be bound, whether there are reasons not to give effect to that intention, and how they could have avoided the dispute. Slide 10 lists possible reasons the parties adopted no third pricing mechanism and asks which of them a court should effectively condone by enforcing the agreement.

topics.heading: Possible legal effects of preliminary statements
topics.body: A preliminary statement may have no legal effect, may be an enforceable agreement subject to formalization (Tribune I) or an enforceable agreement to negotiate in good faith (Tribune II), or may ground promissory estoppel, misrepresentation or promissory fraud. The background rules are that there is no general duty to negotiate in good faith and that restitution may be available for benefits conferred. Slide 12 is images with no text.

topics.heading: Tribune I agreements
topics.body: Slide 14 quotes Teachers Insurance and Annuity Ass'n v. Tribune Co., 670 F. Supp. 491 (S.D.N.Y. 1987): such an agreement exists when the parties have reached complete agreement, including the agreement to be bound, on all issues perceived to require negotiation, and is preliminary only in form. Slide 15 lists factors against binding effect (a disclaimer of intention to be bound, indefiniteness, a complex transaction) and for it (formality, part performance, reliance).

topics.heading: Questions for every preliminary-agreement case
topics.body: Slide 16 asks, for each case: what promise is the claimant enforcing; is it definite enough; are assent and consideration present; was it breached; what is the remedy; is promissory estoppel available; how could the parties have avoided the dispute and how should they behave going forward; and would French law differ?

topics.heading: French Civil Code Article 1112
topics.body: Slide 17 quotes Article 1112 (2016): starting, continuing and breaking off precontractual negotiations are free from control but must satisfy good faith, and reparation for fault during negotiations is not calculated to compensate the benefits expected from the contract that was not concluded.

topics.heading: Channel Home Centers, Cyberchron and Dixon
topics.body: Slide 18 quotes the Channel Home letter of intent, including the promise to “withdraw the Store from the rental market, and only negotiate the above described leasing transaction to completion.” Slide 19 quotes the Cyberchron testimony that Grumman's Wilhelm told Cyberchron to proceed and that issues would be resolved later, while refusing to put it in writing. Slide 20 quotes Dixon: Wells Fargo “made a specific promise to consider the Dixons’ eligibility for a loan modification” if they defaulted and submitted financial information.

topics.heading: Recap of formation
topics.body: Slide 21 sums up whether there is an enforceable promise: offer and acceptance, consideration and definiteness at common law; UCC §§ 2-204 to 2-207 for sales of goods; promissory estoppel; RLCC § 2 for consumer contracts; and the Statute of Frauds for selected transactions. Its applications so far are the battle of the forms, terms that follow, and preliminary negotiations.

topics.heading: Alaska Packers v. Domenico
topics.body: The slides ask what the original terms and the modification were, why the court refused enforcement, whether reliance mattered, and what if the nets were defective or the workers believed they were. Later versions add whether the workers could have given consideration, why they did not make pay conditional on the nets, why Alaska Packers agreed, and how the decision affects future workers' incentives to threaten to quit, neglect the nets, and negotiate wages at the outset.

topics.heading: The pre-existing duty rule
topics.body: Slide 5 quotes Restatement § 73: performing a legal duty owed to the promisor that is neither doubtful nor in honest dispute is not consideration. Mutual promises to rescind are supported by consideration, so the rule does not stop parties from rescinding and replacing a contract, and a modification supported by even minimal consideration is enforceable under the pre-existing duty rule.

topics.heading: Holdup and the economics of modification
topics.body: Slide 7 supposes a cannery that has invested $150,000, holds perishable fish worth $1M and owes $10,000 in wages, and asks the most it should pay if workers threaten to quit (assuming they are judgment-proof) and the least the workers should accept; the amounts are left blank. Slide 9 says enforceability may cut drafting costs at the outset, presumably makes parties better off at the time of modification, and may protect reliance; but a successful holdup gives incentives to bluff, shirk and lowball, which are arguably coercive, unfair and inefficient, and their anticipation may discourage contracting.

topics.heading: Watkins & Son v. Carrig
topics.body: The slide asks about the original terms and the claimed modification, how the defendant resisted enforcement and how the court justified it, and varies the facts: an exorbitant modified price, or a defendant who said “I don’t want to do this, but if you insist…”. It asks why the defendant agreed and what it should do in future.

topics.heading: Modern doctrine: Restatement § 89, statutes and waiver
topics.body: Under § 89 a modification of a contract not fully performed on either side binds if fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated when the contract was made, to the extent a statute provides (UCC § 2-209 and N.Y. Gen. Oblig. L. § 5-1103 remove the consideration requirement), or to the extent justice requires because of a material change of position in reliance. Legal qualification: UCC § 2-209(1) removes the consideration requirement only for modifications of contracts within Article 2 (goods), and the modification must still meet the Code's test of good faith (comment 2); N.Y. Gen. Oblig. L. § 5-1103 applies only to a modification in writing signed by the party against whom it is enforced or by that party's agent. Modifications may also be enforced as waivers, but only until retracted unless relied on.

topics.heading: Ways to forestall modification
topics.body: Contractual limits on modification are ineffective (“Those who make a contract may unmake it”), but no-oral-modification clauses are made effective by statutes such as UCC § 2-209 and N.Y. Gen. Oblig. L. § 15-301, though they may be read narrowly in light of waiver and estoppel. Legal qualification: under UCC § 2-209(2) the clause must be in a signed agreement, and, except as between merchants, a clause on a form supplied by a merchant binds the other party only if that party signs it separately. Other tools are limits on agents' authority and commitments to transfer value to third parties if a modification occurs, such as most-favoured-nation clauses.

topics.heading: Duress and good faith
topics.body: Duress requires an improper threat, which once meant unlawful confinement or bodily harm and now extends to property and economic harm, including breach of contract and a threat to breach the duty of good faith; the absence of a reasonable alternative; and unfair terms, which matter less if the threat is improper enough. Legal qualification: Restatement § 175(1) does not list unfair terms as an element; they are required only for threats that are improper under § 176(2), while a threat listed in § 176(1), such as a threat to breach the duty of good faith and fair dealing, is improper whatever the terms. A threat to breach “without legitimate commercial reason” can be a breach of the duty of good faith (UCC § 2-209, comment 2).

topics.heading: Austin Instrument v. Loral
topics.body: The slide asks what doctrine decided enforceability, how the court defined economic duress and what made the threat wrongful, what if the modification had been prompted by a cost increase, why Loral's alternatives were inadequate, and what Austin would have done had it known the modification would be unenforceable.

topics.heading: Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 3
topics.body: A modification of a standard term in a consumer contract is effective if the consumer gets reasonable notice and opportunity to review, a reasonable opportunity to reject or terminate without unreasonable cost, and assents or fails to reject (Legal qualification: in both editions the consumer must be offered the chance to reject and continue under the existing term; an opportunity to terminate can replace it only under a reasonable modification procedure the contract itself establishes, § 3(b)); the quoted text, from § 3(c) of the 2024 Official Text, adds that it must be proposed in good faith, be fair and equitable in view of unanticipated circumstances (a requirement absent from the Selections' 2019 § 3(c)), and not undermine an affirmation or promise that was part of the basis of the original bargain.

topics.heading: Problem: Hawaiian Housing
topics.body: The figures are a $49K subcontractor bid renegotiated to $62K, an architect's estimate of $16K and other bids of $83K to $173K. The slide asks whether there was consideration, whether this was a fair and equitable response to unanticipated circumstances, and whether there was duress or bad faith.

topics.heading: Misrepresentation as a defence and its policies
topics.body: Slide 2 adds misrepresentation to duress as a defence under the question whether there is an enforceable promise. The class covers misrepresentation and related claims, opinion and puffery, non-disclosure and disclaimers. Slide 4 lists the policy considerations: the immorality of deliberate deception, the unfairness of unequal access to information, and the value of preventing mistaken transactions.

topics.heading: Misrepresentation and related claims
topics.body: Slide 5's table gives key elements and remedies. Fraudulent misrepresentation needs a knowing or reckless false statement and justifiable reliance; negligent misrepresentation a false statement without reasonable basis, a special relationship and justifiable reliance; promissory fraud a fraudulent misrepresentation of intention about future conduct and justifiable reliance. All three allow avoidance and damages in tort. Innocent misrepresentation (a false statement or omission of material fact, with justifiable reliance) allows avoidance but not damages. Breach of warranty (an untrue affirmation or promise that is part of the basis of the bargain) allows damages, and avoidance if material.

topics.heading: Assertions of opinion: Restatement §§ 168 and 169
topics.body: An assertion is opinion if it expresses only a belief, without certainty, about a fact, or a judgment about quality, value or authenticity; where reasonable, the recipient may read it as asserting that the speaker knows no incompatible facts, or knows facts sufficient to justify it. Reliance on pure opinion is not justified unless the recipient is in a relation of trust and confidence with the speaker, reasonably believes the speaker has special skill, judgment or objectivity, or is for some other reason particularly susceptible.

topics.heading: Speakers of Sport v. ProServ and puffing
topics.body: The slide asks on what grounds Speakers of Sport sued, what the relevant promise was, what the false statements or undisclosed facts were, what puffing is according to Posner, and why puffing is not actionable.

topics.heading: Vokes v. Arthur Murray
topics.body: The slide asks what the false statements or undisclosed facts were, what remedy Mrs. Vokes sought, what features made the case an exception to the rules limiting liability for opinion and puffing, and what incentives the ruling creates for dance studios. Slide 10 carries only a headline: “Hong Kong banker wins back millions for dance lessons.”

topics.heading: Liability for non-disclosure
topics.body: At common law silence is treated as an assertion in cases of concealment, failure to correct a previous assertion (a half-truth), a fiduciary duty or relation of trust and confidence, and “failure to act in good faith and in accordance with reasonable standards of fair dealing” (Restatement § 161). Statutes also effectively impose liability for non-disclosure, for example securities, franchising and truth-in-lending laws. Slide 17 adds to the misrepresentation policies the incentives to acquire and use information, the costs of disclosure, and litigation costs.

topics.heading: Swinton v. Whitinsville Savings Bank
topics.body: The slide asks what the undisclosed facts were, what remedy the buyer sought, the rationale for the decision and the countervailing moral argument, what incentives it creates for uninformed buyers and whether they are efficient, what incentives liability for non-disclosure would create, and how uninformed buyers can contract around the rule. Slide 14 gives the broad warranties a buyer can seek, such as “There are no material defects in this house.”

topics.heading: Kannavos v. Annino
topics.body: The slide asks what the false statements or undisclosed facts were, why Swinton did not bar the claim and whether it was overruled, what incentives the decision creates and whether they are efficient, why due diligence was not required, and how sellers can contract around the rule. Slide 16 quotes a sample “AS IS” clause disclaiming all express and implied warranties.

topics.heading: Psenicska v. Twentieth Century Fox and fraud disclaimers
topics.body: The slide asks what the plaintiffs claimed, whether the release barred the claims, the basis for fraudulent inducement, which provisions limited liability for fraud, whether the plaintiffs assented to them, and whether Fox had legitimate reasons to use them. Slide 19 quotes the merger clause, the statement of non-reliance and the waiver of claims of fraud “such as any alleged deception or surprise about this film”.

topics.heading: Should it be possible to contract out of liability for fraud?
topics.body: Slide 20 says it is typically fair and efficient for the maker of a representation to bear the risk of known inaccuracies because it can mitigate the risk at low cost, while respect for party autonomy favours enforcing opt-outs. Limiting liability may be efficient to limit litigation costs, especially if non-legal sanctions are potent, and to limit agency costs.

topics.heading: Sources of terms
topics.body: Slide 2 places the class under whether the contract has been performed: sources of terms, rules of construction and the hierarchy of sources. Terms may be express (writings, or extrinsic evidence of the parties' agreement), implied by law, or drawn from custom, course of dealing and course of performance; the slide notes the procedural implications of considering extrinsic evidence. Slides 5 and 6 return to Bayliner and UCC § 2-314 from Class 1.

topics.heading: What extrinsic evidence can and cannot do
topics.body: Extrinsic evidence cannot vary or contradict an integrated (final) writing, add to a completely integrated (final, complete and exclusive) writing within its scope, or explain an unambiguous agreement. It can be used to invalidate or reform a writing, show grounds for a remedy, establish a collateral agreement beyond the writing's scope or naturally omitted from it, establish the meaning of an ambiguous writing, explain or supplement it through commercial context, and show that performance is subject to a condition.

topics.heading: Terminology and effect of integration
topics.body: Slide 8's table maps Restatement and UCC § 2-202 terms. A partially integrated (“final”) writing discharges prior inconsistent agreements (§§ 213(1), 215) but can be supplemented by consistent additional terms (§ 216(1)). A completely integrated (“final, complete and exclusive”) writing also discharges prior consistent agreements within its scope (§ 213(2)) and cannot be supplemented by consistent additional terms within its scope; under UCC § 2-202(a), course of performance, course of dealing and usage of trade may still explain or supplement it. A merger clause is relevant to the extent of integration but not dispositive, and parol evidence can still challenge the validity of a completely integrated agreement. Legal qualification: courts are split on merger clauses. Some treat the clause as conclusive proof that the writing is completely integrated, while others treat it as strong but rebuttable evidence (C&M 542).

topics.heading: Contentious issues and consumer contracts
topics.body: Slide 10 asks whether the rule should apply to consumer contracts, and whether extrinsic evidence can decide whether a writing is integrated, whether it is ambiguous, and whether commercial context can always explain or supplement it. Slide 11 quotes RLCC § 9 (2024 Official Text; § 8 in the 2019 Tentative Draft in the Selections): a standard term that contradicts, unreasonably limits or fails to give the reasonably expected effect to a business's prior affirmation or promise is not a final expression of the agreement on that subject and does not discharge the obligation.

topics.heading: Policy considerations
topics.body: The benefits listed are a cautionary effect, a reduced risk of interpretive error (writings are easier to interpret, and juries may be biased), reduced reading costs and reduced litigation costs. The competing considerations are increased drafting costs and frustration of the intentions of unsophisticated parties.

topics.heading: Psenicska and fraud under the parol evidence rule
topics.body: Slides 13 to 15 return to Psenicska from Class 12, adding whether the parol evidence rule barred the fraud claim, and repeat the merger, non-reliance and waiver clauses and the arguments for and against contracting out of fraud liability.

topics.heading: Gianni v. R. Russel & Co.
topics.body: The slide asks how the plaintiff wanted to use the parol evidence, whether and to what extent the lease was integrated, how the court decided that and whether it fits Restatement § 214. It varies the facts (the promise in a letter sent before or after the lease was signed) and asks the policy justification for the result, given that the evidence was apparently credible, and what incentives it creates.

topics.heading: Masterson v. Sine
topics.body: The slide asks how the trustee's and the Mastersons' parol evidence was used, how Traynor and Burke treated it, whether and to what extent the deed was integrated and how the court decided, what policy concerns the majority raises, and how parties in California can preclude consideration of parol evidence.

topics.heading: Bollinger v. Central Pennsylvania Quarry
topics.body: The slide asks how the plaintiff wanted to use the parol evidence, whether and to what extent the agreement was integrated, why the evidence was not barred, and the policy justification for that exception.

topics.heading: International approaches and TeeVee Toons
topics.body: CISG Article 8(3) contains no parol evidence rule; the CISG governs international sales of goods between parties whose places of business are in different states when both states are parties to the CISG or the contract is governed by the law of a state party to the CISG, and the US has ratified it. In English law the rule is more like a rebuttable presumption that the writing is complete. On TeeVee Toons the slide asks why the CISG applied, what TVT sought to enforce and with what evidence, how New York law would resolve it, what the court decided, and how the parties could have precluded parol evidence.

topics.heading: Extrinsic evidence and the plain meaning rule
topics.body: The class covers types of ambiguity, rules of construction, California's and New York's approaches to the plain meaning rule, and policy considerations. Slides 3 and 15 repeat the Class 13 summary: extrinsic evidence cannot vary an integrated writing, supplement a completely integrated one within its scope, or explain an unambiguous agreement, but can establish the meaning of ambiguous writings, supplement or qualify through commercial context, establish a collateral agreement beyond the writing's scope or one that might naturally be omitted from it, and establish a condition, and can invalidate or reform a writing. Slides 16 and 17 repeat the contentious issues and the policy considerations.

topics.heading: Ambiguity and vagueness
topics.body: A word, phrase, sentence or clause is ambiguous if it has more than one sense, and vague when it has borderline cases. The examples are a technician who will not compete “within fifty miles of the Company office” (a site 45 miles as the crow flies but 55 by road) and a photo-studio seller who will not compete “in any school in Grant county” except two named high schools (does it reach Marion College?). The slide does not say which example illustrates which. Slides 6 and 7 are images with no text.

topics.heading: Structural (syntactic) ambiguity
topics.body: The casebook's covenant (p. 566) bars managing for any firm that was a client within a year before termination “or with whom you may have been negotiating ... if I have participated in such negotiations or had contact with that firm”. Slide 8 asks about an employee who joins a firm that was a client three months earlier but with which she had no contact; Slides 9 to 11 break the clause into its parts. The speaker note on Slide 11 says the decision favoured “this interpretation” because the alternative would make one clause redundant and might be so broad as to contravene public policy, since the restriction on former clients would be unqualified; which reading the slide highlights is not in the text.

topics.heading: Rules of construction
topics.body: Slide 12 quotes International Fidelity Insurance Co. v. County of Rockland, 98 F. Supp. 2d 400, 412 (S.D.N.Y. 2000): sophisticated lawyers are presumed to know how to use parallel and different wording and the maxim expressio unius est exclusio alterius. Slide 13 lists the rules: purpose; reading the contract as a whole, consistently and giving meaning to every term; the public interest; ejusdem generis; expressio unius; noscitur a sociis; and contra proferentem, “often described as a last resort”.

topics.heading: Problem: the animal-loving tenant
topics.body: Based on the problem at p. 569, a prospective farm tenant owns sheep, cows, pigs, cats and dogs. The slide asks whether the lease should permit “animals”, “sheep, cows, and pigs” or “sheep, cows, pigs and other animals”, and what happens if she wants a guinea pig, a wild boar or a tiger, recalling ejusdem generis, expressio unius, noscitur a sociis and contra proferentem.

topics.heading: Pacific Gas & Electric v. G.W. Thomas Drayage
topics.body: The indemnity covered “all loss, damage, expense and liability resulting from...injury to property arising out of or in any way connected with the performance of this contract.” The slide asks what meaning the defendant gave the provision, what evidence it offered, how Traynor justified admitting that evidence, and the countervailing policy concerns.

topics.heading: Trident Center v. Connecticut General
topics.body: The note said the maker “shall not have the right to prepay the principal amount hereof in whole or in part” for the first 12 years. The slide asks what meaning Trident gave it and with what evidence, whether PG&E requires admitting all such evidence, whether Trident is likely to win, whether the rule fits the parties' intentions, whether it makes more sense for foreign borrowers, and whether California parties can opt out of the PG&E rule.

topics.heading: W.W.W. Associates v. Giancontieri
topics.body: The clause let “either party” cancel if the litigation was not concluded by 6-1-87. The slide asks what meaning the plaintiff gave it, how the plaintiffs sought to use extrinsic evidence, whether the result would differ under California law, and how the court's reasoning differed from California's.

topics.heading: Greenfield v. Philles Records
topics.body: Slide 21 quotes the grant making all recordings and performances Philles' property, with the right to reproduce them “by any method now or hereafter known”. Slide 22 asks what meaning the plaintiffs gave it, whether it is ambiguous (including under California law), why the 1974 release did not bar the claim, the policy justifications, and how the Ronettes could have protected themselves. Slide 23 quotes Judge Graffeo that the royalty schedule does not limit ownership and that the court must “neutrally apply the rules of contract interpretation” despite the plaintiffs' plight.

topics.heading: Commercial context and a final writing
topics.body: Use UCC §§ 1-303(d)–(e) and 2-202 together. Commercial context can explain or supplement a final writing and can qualify its terms. Reconcile the sources whenever reasonable. If they conflict, express terms take priority, then course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade.

topics.heading: Identify the source of the practice
topics.body: Course of performance concerns repeated occasions under the disputed transaction and the other party’s knowing acceptance or acquiescence. Course of dealing concerns prior transactions between the parties. Usage of trade is a regularly observed practice proved as a fact. Examine the parties’ trade or awareness and the place of performance.

topics.heading: Interpretation, waiver, and modification
topics.body: Repeated performance can show what an agreement has meant from the start, or show that a party gave up or changed a right under an express term. Under UCC § 1-303(f), even inconsistent conduct can support waiver or modification. A waiver affecting future performance can ordinarily be retracted by reasonable notice unless reliance would make retraction unjust.

topics.heading: Frigaliment and Hurst on specialized meaning
topics.body: Frigaliment tested the disputed meaning of chicken against incorporated government standards, market price, communications, and evidence of trade practice. The buyer failed to establish its narrower reading. Hurst allowed evidence that the trade rounded protein measurements even though the percentage in the written specification appeared exact.

topics.heading: Apply each party’s knowledge at formation
topics.body: Restatement §§ 20 and 201 ask who knew or had reason to know of the competing meaning. A party less aware of the mismatch can prevail when the other had the corresponding knowledge. Materially different readings can defeat mutual assent when neither party knew or should have known of the other’s meaning, or when both did.

topics.heading: When trade practice qualifies price, quantity, or remedies
topics.body: Nanakuli allowed evidence of price protection and the parties’ performance to support a limited qualification of posted prices. Columbia Nitrogen allowed evidence about flexibility in price and quantity despite a detailed writing. Figgie used proof of a trade practice to supply an exclusive remedy, and the refund fulfilled that remedy.

topics.heading: Drafting around commercial practices
topics.body: Davis compares a targeted no-waiver provision with an express exclusion of course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade. Ask what a merger clause excludes and whether the parties carefully negated the specific practice asserted. The policy tradeoff is between predictable written terms and the cost of specifying every shared convention.

conflicts.heading: Plain meaning depends on the governing approach
conflicts.body: Slide 4 puts explanation of unambiguous language in its exclusion list, then separately permits commercial context to establish meaning. Slides 19–20 show the UCC distinction. Treat the exclusion as a feature of a restrictive interpretive approach. Commercial context under §§ 1-303 and 2-202 does not require an ambiguity found from the writing alone.

topics.heading: Good faith constrains performance and enforcement
topics.body: UCC § 1-304 imposes good faith in performing and enforcing every contract or duty within the Code; § 1-302(b) bars disclaiming it but lets the parties set standards for measuring it that are not manifestly unreasonable. The model definition, § 1-201(b)(20), is honesty in fact and the observance of reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing; New York and several other states kept the older honesty-only definition. Restatement § 205 connects performance and enforcement to the agreed purpose and the parties’ justified expectations.

topics.heading: Use the obligation the parties created
topics.body: Good faith is especially useful when a party can control quantity, satisfaction of a condition, or royalty-generating distribution. Begin with the bargain and the discretion it leaves. The slides distinguish this inquiry from fiduciary loyalty, tort liability, and a separate best-efforts promise.

topics.heading: Dalton and promised consideration of evidence
topics.body: ETS’s promise to accept relevant information required meaningful consideration and a nonarbitrary decision. The New York Court of Appeals did not require ETS to investigate externally or validate the score. It ordered reconsideration under the promised process. Slide 12 compares that implication with later SAT language that expressly requires considering submissions.

topics.heading: Market Street and opportunistic performance
topics.body: Under a lease financing clause, failed negotiations could trigger a valuable purchase option. Posner asked whether the tenant deliberately induced or exploited the pension trust’s oversight. The court remanded because intent remained disputed. The drafting hypotheticals compare an unconditional option, an express notice condition, and a rule keyed to trickery.

topics.heading: Bloor and the evidence of best efforts
topics.body: Falstaff promised best efforts to promote Ballantine sales and owed a royalty tied to volume. The sales graph compares Ballantine’s steep decline with Falstaff and other brewers. The court looked at the distribution decisions and manageable steps Falstaff could have considered while allowing it to protect its own financial viability.

topics.heading: Northwest and federal preemption
topics.body: The Airline Deregulation Act displaced Ginsberg’s Minnesota implied-covenant claim because the state imposed the obligation and the claim related to airline rates or services. Identify any independently enforceable promise the airline actually undertook. The distinction matters where a frequent-flyer program gives the airline broad discretion.

topics.heading: Compare the Commonwealth authorities
topics.body: Ng Giap Hon rejected a general implied duty under Singapore law. The assigned comparative notes use English and Canadian authorities to test narrower controls on contractual discretion and dishonest performance. Identify the particular jurisdiction, duty, and contract power when drawing comparisons.

conflicts.heading: The Dalton cancellation clause is reversed on slide 11
conflicts.body: The written bulletin gave ETS a right to cancel a score when it had reason to question validity, subject to the promised process. The slide’s phrase “right to refuse to cancel” reverses the reservation. The casebook at p. 720 and 87 N.Y.2d at 387 supply the correct clause.

topics.heading: Standardization, consent, and the informed minority
topics.body: Standard forms save negotiation and drafting costs, while limited choice and low attention can weaken the market’s discipline. Davis pairs a software study finding almost nobody opened the license with a separate study finding that later-delivered software terms were no worse by its measure. Each study answers a different question in a particular market.

topics.heading: Late terms require notice and a practical opportunity to exit
topics.body: RLCC § 2(b) asks what the customer was told before committing, whether the customer could review the late term, and whether the customer could end the transaction afterward without unreasonable cost, loss of value, or burden. Under the 2024 Official Text the business must establish these facts; the Selections' 2019 § 2(b) states the same conditions without assigning the burden. Apply that framework separately from the governing law in Carnival.

topics.heading: Consumer assurances and the parol-evidence rule
topics.body: RLCC §§ 8 and 9 (2024 Official Text; §§ 7 and 8 in the 2019 Tentative Draft in the Selections) protect qualifying precontract factual assurances and promises. A boilerplate term may fail to limit the resulting obligation, and an inconsistent term may fail to constitute a final expression on that subject. Identify the business’s specific assurance and the standard term invoked against it.

topics.heading: Reasonable expectations and standardized assent
topics.body: Restatement § 211 generally recognizes assent to the standard writing and favors treating similarly situated parties alike. A term drops out where the drafter had reason to believe the customer would withhold assent if aware of it. Consider negotiations, conspicuous language, commercial context, and an unusual or oppressive provision.

topics.heading: Graham and Carnival test different controls
topics.body: Graham treats even a sophisticated concert promoter as an adherent where the union form was effectively unavoidable. Industry expectations supported arbitration, while the union’s control over the arbitrator made the term unenforceable. Carnival reviews a cruise-ticket forum clause for fundamental fairness and treats notice as conceded on its record.

topics.heading: Statutory policing in the United States and Europe
topics.body: Doe illustrates how a dating-services statute can mandate disclosures, cancellation rights, and other minimum protections. The EU directive pairs understandable drafting with review of significant imbalance in standard terms. Compare these rules with case-by-case assent, expectations, and fairness review.

topics.heading: Contract remedies when a mandatory duty is preempted
topics.body: The class opens by revisiting Ginsberg. Identify express obligations a customer could still invoke when federal law preempts a state-imposed implied covenant. Evaluate those obligations alongside the terms prescribing the airline’s own exercise of discretion.

conflicts.heading: Carnival did not decide when the Shutes assented
conflicts.body: Slides 16–17 invite applying the later-term notice framework as a classroom hypothetical. The Supreme Court’s majority treated notice as conceded and had no occasion to decide adequacy of notice. The dissent discussed receipt after payment and the practical ability to cancel. The July 2019 and 2021 market-share graph is a later comparator.

conflicts.heading: The EU annex identifies candidates for review
conflicts.body: Slide 19’s reference to arbitration is shorthand. Directive 93/13/EEC, Article 3 and Annex 1(q), identify terms that impede legal remedies, including certain compulsory arbitration provisions, as potentially unfair. The annex is indicative and requires assessment under the directive and relevant implementing law.

topics.heading: Test choice and the substance of the bargain
topics.body: Williams asks about meaningful choice and terms unreasonably favorable to the other side. Consider the opportunity to understand the terms, relative bargaining power and realistically available alternatives. Evaluate substantive harshness in light of the transaction and commercial setting.

topics.heading: Williams and cross-collateral repossession
topics.body: Installment payments were spread across outstanding purchases, leaving each item subject to repossession until the total balance was paid. The majority recognized unconscionability review and remanded for findings. The dissent emphasized apparent knowledge and possible effects on access to credit.

topics.heading: Stoll and an oppressive additional term
topics.body: After agreeing to a substantial price for the real estate, the buyers purportedly gave the seller rights to poultry litter for thirty years. Test procedural unfairness through the buyers’ ability to understand the clause, and substantive unfairness through its economic value and duration.

topics.heading: Choose the remedy after finding unconscionability
topics.body: UCC § 2-302 and Restatement § 208 allow refusing enforcement, enforcing the remainder without the term, or limiting the term to avoid an unconscionable result. Davis considers several replacement rules and asks how each allocation affects incentives to draft aggressive terms.

topics.heading: Compare ex ante statutory protection
topics.body: The EU directive uses transparency and substantive unfairness controls. Doe illustrates targeted mandatory protections such as a cooling-off period and required disclosures. Compare the difficulty of proving unfairness case by case with the costs and benefits of setting the obligation in advance.

topics.heading: Anderson separates amendment, temporal scope, and fairness
topics.body: Evaluate whether Binance gave adequate notice of the arbitration amendment, whether its terms reached existing disputes, and whether the heading actually waived class proceedings in court. The assigned 2026 order rejected arbitration and the purported waiver for the remaining pre-amendment claims. The RLCC and EU questions are comparative applications.

conflicts.heading: The four replacement options are classroom alternatives
conflicts.body: Slide 11 presents alternative ways to respond to an unconscionable term. UCC § 2-302 and Restatement § 208 expressly authorize refusal, severance, and limiting application to avoid an unconscionable result. The slide’s least-favorable substitution is a policy option and requires independent support under the governing law.

conflicts.heading: An arbitration clause is not categorically on an EU blacklist
conflicts.body: Slide 13 pairs arbitration with the indicative EU annex. Article 3 and Annex 1(q) call for assessing whether the clause hinders legal remedies. Individual jurisdictions may impose stronger rules. Anderson itself concerns notice, amendment scope, and ambiguous drafting under U.S. law.

topics.heading: Tie unenforceability to a specific policy
topics.body: Identify a statute or recognized policy and how the bargain implicates it. The connection differs when performance itself is unlawful, an otherwise lawful bargain was procured unlawfully, or performance of a lawful promise facilitates another party’s wrongful conduct.

topics.heading: Distinguish enforcement, severance, restitution, and equitable relief
topics.body: Compare the interests supporting enforcement with the strength of the policy, the relationship between the misconduct and the bargain, and the risk of forfeiture. Then consider severance and restitution independently. Relative culpability and unclean hands can affect the availability of particular remedies.

topics.heading: Blossom Farm and X.L.O. Concrete mark different links to illegality
topics.body: Blossom Farm involved a seller knowingly helping the buyer’s continuing mislabeling scheme. X.L.O. Concrete required a developed record on whether payment for construction would enforce the anticompetitive arrangement itself. The extent of the connection matters to deterrence and the risk of a forfeiture unrelated to the policy.

topics.heading: Bribery and transnational public policy
topics.body: In World Duty Free v. Kenya, the arbitral tribunal refused to enforce a concession procured by bribing the head of state. Davis asks how the tribunal identified transnational public policy, what weight a claimed local custom could have, and how denying enforcement affects incentives for firms and states.

topics.heading: Noncompetes and the rule of reason
topics.body: Analyze the underlying transaction, legitimate interests, and the restriction’s duration, geographic reach, and activities covered. Account for hardship to the worker and harm to the public. The slides compare employee, business-sale, and partnership covenants, then use survey evidence and examples to examine effects on competition and information sharing.

topics.heading: Hassler and the refusal to rewrite
topics.body: The Wyoming Supreme Court declined to reshape a covenant with unreasonable time and geographic limits despite a clause asking the court to substitute the maximum permissible restraint. The example exposes the incentive to draft broadly if courts routinely rescue overreaching terms.

topics.heading: Federal rule removal and state-law variation
topics.body: The FTC removed its Non-Compete Rule from the Code of Federal Regulations effective February 12, 2026 following judicial vacatur. Davis compares California’s general prohibition with Massachusetts’s qualified notice, consideration, duration, and other requirements. Verify the governing jurisdiction and agreement date before applying either model.

conflicts.heading: Hardship and public injury are not cumulative requirements
conflicts.body: Slide 15’s list can be read to require excessive scope, undue hardship, and public injury together. Restatement § 188 instead treats a restraint as unreasonable if it is greater than needed to protect a legitimate interest, or if the promisee’s need is outweighed by the hardship to the promisor and likely public injury. Governing statutes can replace the common-law test.

conflicts.heading: Massachusetts uses business-day notice and a qualified duration cap
conflicts.body: Slide 18’s 10-day and 12-month bullets compress Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 149, § 24L(b)(i)–(iv). Notice periods use business days. Mid-employment agreements require independent fair consideration, and the duration can reach two years for specified breaches of fiduciary duty or unlawful taking of employer property.

conflicts.heading: Wyoming later changed the statutory baseline
conflicts.body: Hassler remains the assigned 2022 decision. For contracts entered into on or after July 1, 2025, Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-108 generally voids covered labor noncompetes, subject to its enumerated exceptions. 2025 Wyoming Session Laws ch. 170 preserves contracts entered into before that date from the new act.

topics.heading: An event can be a duty, a condition or a timing marker
topics.body: Ask whether the event is promised, whether another duty depends on its occurrence and whether the language merely fixes when payment comes due. The shipping exercise can be drafted as a promise to sail with the next wind, as a trigger for a premium, or as both. Peacock treated the ambiguous payment clause as determining reasonable timing and required clear language to shift the owner’s credit risk to subcontractors.

topics.heading: The precise financing condition matters
topics.body: Luttinger compares the loan the parties specified with the more expensive financing the buyers could actually obtain. The seller’s offer to subsidize the difference did not turn that loan into a qualifying commitment. Analyze due diligence separately from whether the condition occurred and ask whose protection the condition serves in the cash-purchase hypothetical.

topics.heading: Waiver, prevention and forfeiture
topics.body: Separate an advance waiver, an election to go forward after failure, and an agreed modification. Material contribution to nonoccurrence through breach can excuse a condition under § 245. Section 229 permits a limited excuse for disproportionate forfeiture when occurrence was not a material part of the exchange.

topics.heading: Satisfaction and good faith
topics.body: Mattei distinguishes objective reasonableness for commercial value or functional fitness from honest subjective dissatisfaction for matters of judgment or taste. The class also asks how an architect’s certification changes the problem. Identify whose satisfaction the contract requires and the standard that governs it.

topics.heading: Constructive conditions and materiality
topics.body: An uncured material failure can excuse the other side’s remaining performance. In Kingston, security for the purchase price had to precede transfer of the business. In Jacob & Youngs, the equivalence of the substituted pipe, the purpose of the specification and the waste of replacing it matter to substantial performance. A monetary allowance for breach remains a separate question.

topics.heading: Dividing performance into agreed equivalents
topics.body: Restatement § 240 asks whether part performances can be paired as agreed equivalents. Gill allowed recovery for logs actually delivered under a unit-price arrangement. The halfway-delivery question tests whether a court can invent a new unit of payment when the parties paired payment with completed delivery.

topics.heading: Net benefit after material breach
topics.body: Nelson tests restitution for the party whose failure prevented recovery of the contract balance. Measure the benefit retained and account for the owner’s payments and losses from the breach. The policy tradeoff is avoiding a windfall while preserving the owner’s protection against defective work.

conflicts.heading: Article 2 rejection and cure
conflicts.body: The slide’s reference to any breach is shorthand for the ordinary perfect-tender rule governing an initial tender. Section 2-601 is subject to agreed limits and installment-contract rules. Account for timely rejection, applicable cure and the distinct rules after acceptance. The deck identifies perfect tender as outside the lecture’s main coverage.

topics.heading: Mistake about meaning and mistake about facts
topics.body: The Peerless hypothetical tests whether materially different meanings prevent assent under § 20. Mistake under §§ 152–154 instead concerns a basic assumption about existing facts. Determine whether the error was mutual or unilateral and, for unilateral mistake, test unconscionability or the other party’s knowledge or fault. Legal qualification: under § 153 the mistaken party must also meet the § 152 requirements and not bear the risk under § 154, and clause (b) is met when the other party had reason to know of the mistake or his fault caused it.

topics.heading: Allocate risk before deciding excuse
topics.body: Risk can follow the parties’ agreement, conscious reliance on limited knowledge or a court’s reasonable allocation. Paradine and Stees illustrate strict enforcement of undertaken duties. The class compares that baseline with presumed intent, fairness and the relative ability to prevent, insure against or absorb the loss.

topics.heading: Renner and the remedy after avoidance
topics.body: The parties shared a material mistake about water availability for jojoba cultivation. Rescission opens an accounting for each side’s transfers or benefits. The buyers’ expenditures on the land matter to restitution to the extent they benefited the sellers. This accounting differs from awarding the profit of the hoped-for venture. Legal qualification: under Arizona law Renner also refused the buyers their development (reliance) costs as consequential damages absent fraud or misrepresentation, and charged them the fair rental value of their occupancy.

topics.heading: Impracticability and the particular means of performance
topics.body: Taylor treats accidental loss of the particular music hall as defeating a basic assumption. Transatlantic tests whether a costlier available route is impracticable. The shipping-risk diagram traces the same loss from higher overall costs to fuel usage, canal closure and its possible causes, showing why how narrowly the risk is framed affects the analysis.

topics.heading: Frustration and the parties’ shared purpose
topics.body: In Krell, the cancellation of the coronation procession defeated the shared foundation of hiring the viewing rooms even though the rooms could be supplied. The taxi comparison asks when a customer’s purpose becomes a basic assumption of the exchange. The pandemic scenario tests whether a different event and contract change the result.

topics.heading: Force majeure turns on the clause’s scope
topics.body: Compare the example covering delays outside a party’s reasonable control with the lease clause permitting temporary excuse but expressly preserving most rent obligations and excluding financing shortfalls. Identify the event, causal link, obligation covered, duration and contractual exceptions before reaching default excuse doctrine.

conflicts.heading: Adjustment after excuse and reformation of a writing
conflicts.body: Slide 11 groups several forms of equitable relief under reformation. Distinguish restitution after avoidance, equitable adjustment after supervening events and reformation of a writing that fails to express the agreement. A material mistake or later event does not automatically authorize a court to rewrite contract terms.

title: Overview of remedies and specific relief

topics.heading: Identify the remedial baseline
topics.body: Expectation asks where performance would have left the promisee. Reliance asks where the promisee would have been without the agreement. Restitution looks to benefits transferred. The lecture also compares possible gain-based, stipulated and punitive remedies as policy alternatives, with their own legal limits.

topics.heading: Adequacy of damages and the equitable inquiry
topics.body: Consider realistic substitute performance, valuation and practical enforceability. The deck treats land as traditionally presumptively unique and uses UCC § 2-716’s uniqueness or other proper circumstances standard for goods. Equitable considerations include delay, fairness and supervision. The CISG discussion adds Article 28’s forum-law qualification.

topics.heading: Personal services and negative injunctions
topics.body: The class tests supervision, hardship and compelled-service concerns where a contract calls for skill and discretion. A negative covenant concerning especially distinctive services can raise a different equitable question. Consider what the requested injunction would require the promisor to do in practice.

topics.heading: Klein and Walgreen on substitute relief
topics.body: Compare an aircraft sale, where comparable replacements and monetary damages were available, with a lease exclusivity clause whose breach would make a decade of competitive losses difficult to estimate. Walgreen compares the cost of measuring damages with the cost of enforcing an injunction and bargaining after it issues.

topics.heading: Same machine allocation, different surplus
topics.body: The worked diagrams send the machine to buyer C under three arrangements. Expectation damages leave the original buyer with $400 and the seller with $500. With specific performance and costless resale or renegotiation at the stated prices, the original buyer receives $600 in surplus and the seller receives $300. The possibility of transfer and the distribution of gains are distinct questions. Legal qualification: if the parties renegotiate instead of reselling, any release payment from $400 to $600 leaves both at least as well off as performance, and where it lands depends on bargaining (C&M 35–36; compare Walgreen's bargaining range, C&M 949).

topics.heading: The limits of efficient breach
topics.body: Expectation damages create the model’s incentive only when actors have suitable information about losses. Bargaining costs, obstacles to resale, reliance incentives and judicial error can change outcomes. The deck treats the preference for expectation damages as a policy hypothesis to test.

topics.heading: Cosby and reliance on a government assurance
topics.body: The lecture tests promise, authority, reliance and remedy using § 90 as a framework for discussion. The court’s actual ground was fundamental fairness after a nonprosecution assurance induced surrender of the privilege against self-incrimination. The remedy enforced the assurance by barring retrial.

title: Losing contracts and the cost or value of performance

topics.heading: Price the performance baseline
topics.body: The surgery table contrasts the position without the agreement, the position with promised performance and the actual result. For expectation, start with the lost value of what was promised, subtract costs or losses avoided, and add other recoverable losses such as corrective treatment where supported. The table is a classroom hypothetical drawn loosely from Sullivan.

topics.heading: Algernon Blair and the loss-making bargain
topics.body: A subcontractor that stopped after a material breach could seek the reasonable value of the labor and equipment supplied. The class compares that result with expectation on an unprofitable subcontract and asks how it affects a prime contractor’s incentive to substitute a cheaper performer.

topics.heading: Completion cost, market diminution and personal value
topics.body: Each measure asks a different question. Section 348(2) provides alternatives when the injured party’s value loss from defective or unfinished construction cannot be proved with sufficient certainty. Reasonable completion cost is subject to the limit that it not be clearly disproportionate to the probable loss in value to the injured party.

topics.heading: Plante and the misplaced wall
topics.body: Substantial performance let the builder recover the balance subject to deductions. Correcting a wall that caused no demonstrated market loss would require disproportionate work. The deck asks whether either completion cost or market price captures what the promisee personally lost.

topics.heading: Groves, Peevyhouse and the value of restoration
topics.body: Groves allowed a completion-cost measure for deliberate nonperformance of the restoration promise. Peevyhouse limited recovery to market diminution after treating restoration as incidental and its cost as grossly disproportionate. The lecture asks how price, willingness to pay and the parties’ bargaining choices bear on the importance of restoration.

topics.heading: Drafting the restoration bargain
topics.body: The Weevyhouses exercise asks how to make restoration central and protect the landowners before signing. Compare how express restoration milestones, payment security and a defensible agreed remedy address the risk, then analyze completion cost and market diminution if the language is left unchanged.

topics.heading: Alternative purposes of default rules
topics.body: A majoritarian default saves the cost of writing a term many parties want. A penalty default can instead prompt the party with better information to disclose it. The lecture applies that distinction to the incentives created by damages limits, including disclosure, precautions, insurance and agreed damages.

topics.heading: Avoidable loss after a clear breach or repudiation
topics.body: Rockingham limits recovery for expenditures the builder incurred after receiving an unequivocal repudiation. The hypothetical separates suspected cancellation from a clear repudiation and asks how to handle reasonable but unsuccessful efforts to find substitute work. Section 350 accounts for risk, burden, expense and humiliation. Legal qualification: § 350(1) bars only loss the injured party could have avoided without undue risk, burden or humiliation, and § 350(2) preserves recovery to the extent of reasonable but unsuccessful efforts to avoid loss.

topics.heading: Comparable substitute work
topics.body: Parker compares the promised musical role with a substitute western. The majority treated significantly different or inferior work as outside the required mitigation inquiry. The dissent wanted factual evaluation of comparability. The drafted-payment hypothetical asks whether express guaranteed compensation can change the allocation. Legal qualification: the majority held that rejected work reduces damages only if the employer shows it was comparable or substantially similar, so work 'of a different or inferior kind' need not be accepted; asking whether differences were 'substantial enough to constitute differences in the kind of employment' was the dissent's test.

topics.heading: Foreseeability at contract formation
topics.body: Hadley asks whether the loss follows in the ordinary course or from special circumstances the parties had reason to contemplate when they contracted. The discussion tests when a shipping customer must disclose unusual stakes and why learning them only after formation ordinarily does not supply the necessary contemporaneous notice. Legal qualification: the Cold Steel problem asks, without answering, whether knowledge gained when the parties later agreed on a delivery date counts (Spang Industries).

topics.heading: Restatement, CISG and Article 2 formulations
topics.body: The lecture compares Hadley and § 351 with CISG Article 74’s foresight of a possible consequence and UCC § 2-715’s buyer-side consequential-loss inquiry. In Article 2, assess requirements the seller had reason to know and whether cover or another reasonable step could prevent loss. Analyze consequential loss and available market or cover measures separately.

topics.heading: Kenford and assumption of extraordinary loss
topics.body: The county could anticipate that a stadium would affect nearby land values without undertaking liability for lost appreciation. The lecture distinguishes that reasoning from ordinary foreseeability and asks how explicit allocations or damage exclusions could change the result. The casebook notes that Comment 2 to UCC § 2-715 rejects the tacit-agreement test (C&M 1028).

topics.heading: Proof of uncertain profits and lost opportunities
topics.body: Fera asks whether evidence permits a reasonable estimate of the new business’s lost profits. The lecture tests how operating history, comparable stores and disagreement among experts change the proof. The quiz-finalist example compares denial, full-value recovery and probability-weighted recovery as competing approaches to a lost chance.
